plos-pone-0357031:
Clara Rodríguez-Morata leads a team of eight extending a chemical method for dating old wood in PLOS ONE in 2026. Many medieval and early modern timbers across the Euro-Atlantic region have too few rings, or rings that barely vary, for classic tree ring dating. Oxygen isotope ratios in the wood still carry a yearly signal. The team built a three hundred year reference record, spanning 1300 to 1600, for the eastern Netherlands and northwest Germany.

Their reference matched independent isotope records from Belgium and Britain strongly, and French and inland records more weakly. With a local reference in hand, the method dated single timbers with as few as thirty rings. Where no local reference exists, pooling isotope series from three to five timbers of the same age and widening the time window improved success. The study hands conservators a sampling playbook for buildings whose timbers defeat the standard approach.
plos-pone-0358531:
Readers should note first what kind of record this is. In 2026 the PLOS One Editors published a short editorial note, not a new research study. It concerns an earlier article about a lab instrument built to measure twenty-one proteins linked to heart and vessel risk, using a method called Proximity Extension Assay.

An editorial note tells readers that the journal has a concern about the earlier article and is flagging it while the record is clarified. The editors' note does not itself present new data or settle the concern. Anyone citing the CVD-21 instrument study should read this flag first and treat the original claims with added care until the journal updates the record.
plos-pone-0358231:
Alina Pokhrel led a team of six authors studying the genetics of Callery pear trees, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. This pear, widely planted as the Bradford pear in suburbs, has wild kin whose genetic variety is worth saving. The team read markers drawn from the trees' mitochondrial genomes.

Pokhrel and her colleagues used those markers to map how much variety exists and how populations are structured. Such a map tells conservation staff which stands hold rare variants and should be protected first. It also helps explain how this species spread and adapted. Keeping wild diversity alive matters because breeders may need those genes to face new pests or a warming climate.
plos-pone-0358431:
Michael Kalinoski led a team of six authors studying patients who stay critically ill after severe lung failure, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Some intensive care patients with acute hypoxic respiratory failure never turn the corner, entering a state of persistent critical illness. The team reviewed records to describe that group clearly.

Kalinoski's cohort study paints a detailed clinical portrait of these patients and their course. Recognizing the trajectory early helps intensive care teams plan treatment and hold honest talks with families about likely outcomes. Resources in intensive care are precious, and so is hope; knowing which patients face a long, flat course helps match both to reality with more care.
plos-pone-0358331:
JiaLe Yang led a team of five authors profiling the safety of a lung cancer drug, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Entrectinib treats certain non-small cell lung cancers, but trial data cover limited patients. The team mined two adverse event databases, the American FAERS and the Japanese JADER, for real-world safety signals.

Yang's multi-source analysis complements trial findings and sometimes challenges them. Two national databases give a wider view than either alone, catching signals that appear in one population first. Oncologists prescribing entrectinib gain a fuller list of effects to watch and counsel about. Pharmacovigilance work like this is how a drug's true safety profile emerges in the years after approval.
plos-pone-0353031:
Wenbin Xu and coauthors published a 2026 genetics study in PLOS ONE asking whether Crohn's disease and acute pancreatitis share inherited roots. The two conditions, one inflaming the pancreas and one the gut, show similar symptoms and occur together more often than chance would suggest. Using large genome-wide datasets of European ancestry, the team measured genetic correlation, then hunted for shared variants and genes with several statistical methods.

The two diseases did share a modest but real genetic correlation. The hunt turned up dozens of shared variants grouped into six genome regions, with suggestive evidence that one region holds a single causal signal behind both diseases. Eight genes were prioritized, several tied to recycling worn cell parts and fat metabolism, and the shared biology converged on inflammatory pathways, especially one for immune signaling in the gut. This overlap, they say, may explain the comorbidity and hint at shared treatment targets.
plos-pone-0336831:
Agnieszka Turska-Kawa and Irena Pilch published a study in PLOS ONE on why Poland's oldest voters, the grey voters, support populist parties. The focus falls on religion and a group psychology trait called national collective narcissism. That trait means seeing one's nation as superior while demanding others confirm it. The authors tested whether religiosity predicts populist voting, and whether collective narcissism carries part of that effect.

Their results confirmed both links: more religious respondents were more likely to vote populist, and collective narcissism mediated the relationship, channeling part of faith's influence into voting. Religious faith itself predicted populist voting more strongly than religious practice such as attendance did. The authors interpret the pattern within Poland's recent politics, where the long-governing populist party drew heavily on national and religious identity. For students of aging societies, it shows how belief and national pride, not age alone, steer the grey vote.
plos-pone-0355931:
Ebtesam Abdullah Alqhtani and coauthors published a 2026 animal study in PLOS ONE on whether a plant compound can shield the body from microplastic damage. Microplastics are now everywhere, and their health effects are only beginning to be mapped. Rats were exposed for four weeks to tiny polystyrene beads of two sizes, some groups also given puerarin, an isoflavone from kudzu root.

Both bead sizes provoked oxidative stress, raised inflammatory signals, and switched on cell-death proteins, while protective systems faltered: a master antioxidant switch dimmed and a cancer-guardian protein fell. DNA damage appeared as visible comet tails in cell tests. Rats that also received puerarin at the tested dose fared better across those measures, with stress, inflammation, cell death, and DNA damage all eased. Dose-ranging and longer studies are needed before anyone claims a remedy, but a candidate protector against an unavoidable pollutant is identified.
plos-pone-0356631:
Dohee Park and Jong-Hyun Kim tackle a subtle failure in computer hair animation. Filler strands sit between guided strands. They can move too little, because their neighbors' motions cancel out. Standard blending keeps weights between zero and one, which caps expressiveness. Their method borrows from signal processing. It splits strand motion into calm and lively parts. The lively part may overshoot. Safeguards stop strands from stretching absurdly.

Separate settings near roots and tips respect how real hair behaves, steady at the scalp and free at the ends. Park and Kim argue the exaggerated blending restores swaying, overlapping, and splitting that tracking-based animation tends to flatten. The work targets film and game tools where hair should look alive, not pasted on.
plos-pone-0357231:
Shuchang Li and colleagues search public gene datasets for markers of osteoarthritis tied to acetylation, a chemical tagging system that tunes gene activity. The worn-joint disease has few early blood or tissue tests, and tagging may help drive it. Three datasets were mined for changed genes, network analysis found the modules that move together, and machine learning distilled candidate markers, with the winners checked in lab assays on real tissue.

Two well-known growth genes emerged as the markers, both turned down in diseased tissue in datasets and in the lab checks. A prediction model built on the pair separated patients from controls strongly in training and moderately in validation. Li and colleagues propose the pair as fresh leads for early detection and for drugs that retune joint cell tags.
plos-pone-0356731:
Yousif Elsamani, Cristian Mejia, and Yuya Kajikawa mapped half a century of innovation research, nearly fifty thousand papers. They hunted for the field's structural blind spot. Their 2026 bibliometric study clustered the citation network and read the landmark works closely. It compared innovation research, which studies systems, against innovativeness research, which studies individual adopters.

The two literatures live at opposite levels, one macro and one micro. The middle level, the organizations and ecosystems where ideas actually scale, stays underbuilt. Well-being is treated as an afterthought almost everywhere. The authors propose an integrated framework spanning all three levels. Well-being, ethics, and sustainability sit at its core as principles, not decorations. Managers and funders get a map of what the field has been missing.
plos-pone-0356531:
Saima Mushtaq and seven colleagues examine the mental health burden of ulcerative colitis in Pakistan in this 2026 study. The disease causes long-term inflammation of the large bowel, and care in Pakistan rarely addresses patients' psychological state. About one hundred patients attending a hospital clinic in Rawalpindi completed standard questionnaires on anxiety, depression, and quality of life, alongside clinical scoring of their disease.

Roughly one patient in five had anxiety, and a similar share had depression. The more severe the bowel disease, the higher the distress and the worse the reported quality of life, with about one patient in eight rating their quality of life as poor. Anxiety and depression themselves predicted worse quality of life even after other factors were considered. The authors call for care that treats the mind alongside the gut.
plos-pone-0351831:
Sayaka Osanami Törngren and co-authors compared how university students define and apply racial categories in three countries: Japan, Sweden, and the United States. Race is often treated as fixed biology, yet everyday sorting may vary by society. Their 2026 study combined written definitions, face-sorting tasks, and eye tracking across the three countries.

Students everywhere defined race mainly by physical traits and by labels imposed from outside. Cultural and ethnic framings appeared unevenly across the settings. The same faces were sorted into different races in different countries, showing how fluid the sorting is. Eye movements, by contrast, showed no attention differences. The authors read the package as strong evidence that racial categorisation bends with context.
plos-pone-0342631:
Adetayo Aborisade and co-authors pooled Nigerian studies on oral hygiene and tooth decay. Cleaning habits and decay are linked everywhere, but a national synthesis was missing. Their 2026 meta-analysis searched six databases for studies from 2001 to 2025 and combined those reporting decay by hygiene status.

Twenty-three studies qualified, most from southern Nigeria. Poor oral hygiene came with roughly double the odds of decay; removing one outlying study softened the figure but kept it strong. Brushing at least twice daily clearly protected teeth. The cleaning tool itself, brush or traditional chewing stick, made no significant difference. Aborisade and colleagues conclude frequency beats equipment in Nigerian decay prevention.
plos-pone-0352031:
Kelli Goodman and co-authors tested whether dried blood spots from cats and dogs keep their chemical fingerprints after three years in a freezer. A dried spot needs only a pinprick, making it cheap and green for animal biobanks. Their 2026 study re-analysed duplicate cards from five breed groups after long storage at deep-freeze temperatures.

The stored spots retained most of their measurable chemicals, losing only a small share of detected compounds. Careful checking blamed the small drop mainly on run-to-run variation rather than decay. A bridging sample design also let separate datasets be combined honestly. Goodman and colleagues judge dried spots suitable for long-term animal biobanking and for reusing older data in new biomarker hunts.
plos-pone-0344331:
Shunuan Xie, Linxiang Guo, and Wen Zhang compare in 2026 how researchers phrase caution and confidence in summaries of materials science articles. They built two matched sets of summaries, one by writers whose first language is Chinese and one by writers whose first language is English. Each set held about five hundred recent summaries.

Chinese first language writers used softening words more often and leaned on a narrow set of them. English first language writers used a wider range of softeners and slightly more strong boosters. Markers of personal stance were alike. The authors link the pattern to both culture and field norms, with lessons for teaching academic English.
plos-pone-0354331:
Kangkang Chang studies in 2026 a mathematical model of West Nile virus that includes random noise, asking when the system settles within a set time. The virus, first found in Uganda, spreads in many regions and still has no specific drug or vaccine. Chang first shows the model's solutions exist, stay bounded, and are unique.

A specially built function and a classic inequality then give a clear condition for stability in finite time. Computer runs backed the maths and showed the roles of noise strength, death rates, and spread rates. Lower noise and spread with higher death rates favoured stability, a guide for judging control options.
plos-pone-0355731:
Sinan Ersan and co-authors review in 2026 why patients seen for eye emergencies at a major trauma centre in Buffalo fail to return for booked follow-up. Eye checks after an emergency can catch worsening disease and even hidden body illness. Records covered several thousand consultations, split by self reported race and by social and medical factors.

More than two in five patients who needed follow-up did not attend. Race itself showed no clear link once other factors were counted. Living where schooling rates were low, waiting longer for the appointment, and having near normal vision all raised the chance of not returning. Diagnosis mattered differently within racial groups.
plos-pone-0354131:
Seo-Yun Choi, Ju Hyun Kim, Soondool Chung, and Yuri Jang published this 2026 study of bladder problems and mood among older Korean Americans in subsidized senior housing nearby. They asked whether bladder leakage leads to depressive symptoms partly by wrecking sleep. Just over three hundred residents, averaging about seventy-nine years old, answered surveys used in mediation analysis.

Leakage and low mood were clearly linked, and poor sleep carried roughly a quarter of that connection. Choi suggests that treating sleep problems could soften the mental health burden of incontinence, a condition many older adults hide rather than report.
plos-pone-0354231:
Brown and colleagues, in a 2026 study, test how reminding voters of Kamala Harris's race and gender shaped views of her during the 2024 presidential race. Harris, the Democratic nominee, carries several identities that were often noted in coverage. The team ran two experiments with American adults before the election.

In the first, people read a short profile stressing either her qualifications alone or her qualifications plus her gender, her race, or both. Mentioning her race made ratings less favorable, no matter the reader's politics. In the second, her background was split apart, and only mention of her Black identity drove the drop; her South Asian identity alone did not. Conservatives also rated her below an unnamed candidate mainly when her Black identity was highlighted. The authors conclude that even quiet identity cues can move candidate ratings, and that one identity can matter far more than others.
plos-pone-0354031:
Kasthuri Arachchi and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask whether a business owner's financial literacy lifts the performance of small and mid-sized firms in Sri Lanka. Such firms drive jobs and growth in developing economies but are held back by thin finance and weak money management. Most literacy research stops at households; this team surveyed more than two hundred sixty owner-managers in the Western Province.

Financial literacy clearly tracked with better firm performance. It also tracked with two stepping stones: adopting financial technology, and gaining access to finance. The authors read the pattern as literacy paying twice, once through sounder daily decisions and risk control, and once by opening doors to tools and credit. They recommend that owners treat financial learning as core training, and that government programs be rebuilt with more depth and practical grip. Current programs are little used by the people inside firms.
plos-pone-0353931:
Huan Song, Yueyu Shu, and Ping Ren trace a chain from brooding thoughts to lower happiness among Chinese vocational college students, in this 2026 PLOS ONE survey study. Four hundred and two students reported on rumination — chewing over problems endlessly — their grip on their emotions, their social media habits, and their overall life satisfaction and mood.

Rumination travelled with worse emotion control and heavier, more problematic social media use, and both of those travelled with lower well-being. The statistical chain ran rumination to emotion trouble to compulsive scrolling to diminished happiness, with each link carrying part of the effect. Interventions, the authors suggest, should teach emotion skills early in the chain rather than scolding students about screen time.
plos-pone-0351331:
Bria Browne and four colleagues use linked English health records to find what sends people with dementia back into hospital, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. More than thirty thousand patients over sixty-five with dementia and an acute hospital stay were followed for readmission within six months, and for death within a year of any readmission. Two in five were readmitted in that window.

Carrying several long-term conditions was the strongest driver of return. Being male raised the odds, while living in residential care lowered them, perhaps because help is on site. After readmission, age dominated the risk of dying. The authors point to community support for people juggling dementia plus multiple illnesses as the place to intervene.
plos-pone-0352431:
Xie and colleagues searched gene data for links between bile acid handling and sepsis in a 2026 study. Sepsis is a runaway body response to infection that can kill quickly. Using public gene data sets, the team found genes tied to bile acid processing that also changed in sepsis.

Network and learning methods narrowed the field to hub genes for a risk prediction model. Immune cell patterns in sepsis samples were examined alongside. Bile acids are best known for digestion, so a strong sepsis link would open fresh thinking about how gut and liver signals shape immune collapse. The model now needs testing in patient samples beyond public data.
plos-pone-0351031:
Yiming Song and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One field study on sweet potato planting. It asks how the cuttings growers plant shape the hormones that drive storage root growth. Trials over two seasons used one cultivar. They compared cuttings with six, eight, or ten nodes. The cuttings were planted slanted or flat, with the tip exposed or buried. The team measured growth hormones inside the buried nodes. They also tracked root growth and final yield.

Longer cuttings rooted faster and yielded much more. Flat planting also beat slanted planting. Two hormones rose in buried nodes as node number grew. Both tracked closely with yield and root traits. Storage roots formed mainly at the upper buried nodes. The best mixes paired eight-node cuttings with flat planting. This gives growers a concrete, low-cost way to lift harvests.
plos-pone-0345431:
Tone Hovda and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One pilot study of breast cancer screening guided by inherited risk rather than age alone. Eighty women in their forties who had been referred for mammography gave DNA samples, from which the team calculated a polygenic risk score combining thousands of small genetic variants. Each woman's estimated ten-year risk was then compared with that of an average woman her age.

Half the women were advised to start regular screening earlier than the standard program, and a few were offered yearly scans because their risk was high. Family history changed advice for some women independently of the genetic score, and gene panel testing in a subgroup found no dangerous variants. Most participants welcomed the assessment and reported no extra anxiety, supporting larger trials of risk-based screening.
plos-pone-0353131:
Junjie Zhang authored this 2026 PLOS One exercise study comparing heavy lifting with light lifting done while blood flow to the muscles is partly restricted. Seventeen college sprinters tried four warm-up routines in random order: heavy or light hip thrusts and half-squats, the light versions paired with restriction cuffs. Five minutes later the researchers tested twenty-meter sprint times, muscle shape, and stiffness.

The light routines with restricted blood flow improved sprint times more than the heavy routines, each helping a different segment of the sprint. Muscle stiffness generally rose after the sessions, and the angle of muscle fibers fell under some conditions. Zhang concludes that light, restricted exercise may prime explosive performance better than heavy loads in the minutes before competition.
plos-pone-0351931:
Botao Yang and three colleagues grade how well basic clinics in Hebei Province, China, combine treatment with prevention. Their 2026 study spans 2017 to 2024. It covers every township health centre and community health service centre in the province. Yearbook data fed an index system built with expert consultation. Statistical models then measured coordination between medical care and public health services.

The verdict is a familiar pattern: high coupling, low coordination. The two service lines are institutionally linked and move together. Yet their joint development stays shallow and uneven. Medical services and prevention pull at different speeds year after year. An obstacle analysis points to the factors holding coordination back. For the Healthy China strategy, the study shows that merging services on paper is the easy part. Making them grow in step is the real work.
plos-pone-0351631:
Kaiming Tao and colleagues tested whether coaching large language models makes them better at answering set questions from full research papers. Their test bed was HIV drug resistance studies, with sixteen fixed questions per paper about sequences, patients, and treatments. They compared three well-known models, then tried extra training on worked examples and a prompting style built from question-specific rules.

Extra training sharpened precision, meaning fewer wrong facts offered, and helped the models in different degrees. The rule-based prompts mainly lifted recall, meaning fewer facts missed, though gains were uneven. Stacking prompts on top of training added nothing further. For teams hoping to mine papers automatically, the study maps which coaching buys which kind of accuracy, in a field where a missed treatment detail can mislead real research.
plos-pone-0347631:
Ahmad Al-Bitar and colleagues surveyed nine hundred sixty medical students across Syria about pornography use, a topic with almost no published data from the Middle East. An anonymous online questionnaire asked about first exposure, current habits, attempts to stop, and perceived effects on mood, study, and sexual life. Medical students were chosen partly because their stress load is thought to raise vulnerability.

Three quarters reported lifetime exposure, first met on average in the mid-teens. About half were current users, and half of those had tried to quit, many reporting irritability, erotic dreams, or broken concentration afterward. Roughly one in eight described themselves as addicted, with very early first exposure the strongest marker. Having a private room and higher family income predicted exposure more than gender did. The study gives Syrian educators a first factual footing on a subject usually governed by silence.
plos-pone-0350231:
Vaccines spoil if they warm up, so the refrigerated chain carrying them matters most where clinics are poorest. Amatullah Sana Qadeer and colleagues reviewed how vaccine supply systems work in low- and middle-income countries, in this 2026 PLOS One scoping review of studies from 2010 to 2025.

Sixteen studies qualified from more than two thousand screened. Systems ranged from central control to local control, some linking records across sites, and many worked partly offline. Common features included automatic stock tracking, personal health records, and digital cards for families. The review maps what helps these systems succeed and where digital tools have actually been adopted.
plos-pone-0351431:
The thalamus, a relay hub deep in the brain, is divided into small nuclei that surgeons and researchers need to locate precisely. Daniel H Nguyen and colleagues revisited an older mapping method that draws borders from wiring patterns, in this 2026 PLOS One study using high-resolution scans from sixty-seven healthy adults.

The wiring-based method, refreshed with sharper data and modern tracing, was compared with three newer techniques. All were checked against three tissue-based atlases and one based on brain activity. Group maps showed where methods agree and where they part. The comparison helps imaging teams choose a segmentation tool knowing its biases, rather than trusting any single map.
plos-pone-0351731:
Many common medicines slow the stomach or loosen the valve above it, causing delayed emptying and reflux. Zhiheng Qian and Ni Jiang mined more than fifty-eight million side-effect reports filed with American regulators since 2004, checking their findings against Canadian data, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Among the fifty most reported drugs, twenty showed consistent warning signals across three statistical methods. A popular class of diabetes and weight drugs showed the strongest links to stomach slowing. Timing analysis described how soon symptoms tended to appear after starting each drug. The authors offer the risk map to help prescribers weigh stomach effects hidden inside long drug lists.
plos-pone-0351131:
A lab-made antibody called iscalimab was meant to calm autoimmunity by blocking a key immune handshake, yet trials in transplantation disappointed. Chelsea Gootjes and colleagues tested a copy of the antibody on T cells in dishes to see whether T cell control was the weak point, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

The antibody bound its targets and completely stopped B cell growth, matching earlier reports. But it barely slowed diabetes-linked T cell clones that attack insulin-making cells, and it did not curb fresh T cell responses either. The authors argue this blind spot may explain the limited clinical benefit seen so far.
plos-pone-0350931:
Solomon Mohammed Salia and colleagues watched newborn care in six health sites in Ghana and scored it against world and national standards. Deaths of newborns in Ghana stay above world averages, and deaths inside facilities have risen. Trained watchers followed just under one hundred and sixty health workers, then met them to check what the scores meant.

Only about one fifth of workers scored well on stopping infections. Roughly half did well on basic care for every newborn and on kind, respectful care. Poorly placed hand washing gear, parent habits for cord care, and a lack of pain check rules were named as blocks. Watching real practice, the authors say, shows gaps that reports alone can hide.
plos-pone-0347231:
Ahmed Sewify and colleagues piloted a method to rebuild the whole shoulder in three dimensions from ultrasound scans. Ultrasound sees only a small, shallow window, so one scan cannot capture the full joint. Five healthy volunteers were scanned with a robot guided probe across five shoulder zones, giving dozens of overlapping volumes, aligned with probe tracking, image matching, and MRI bone guides.

Blended alignment beat probe tracking alone by about seventeen percent in accuracy. Rebuilt shoulders showed cleaner joins and fewer artefacts. Amount of overlap and shifts in shoulder pose between scans mattered most. Full shoulder ultrasound maps could one day guide injections and surgery without radiation, if accuracy holds in patients.
plos-pone-0350731:
Hyeon Jo and Hyunchul Ahn modelled survey data from over twelve thousand solo self employed Koreans in 2020 on digital work and well being. Solo owners face tech pressure without a firms support. The model linked digital uptake, autonomy, work and life spillover, engagement, and burnout with job satisfaction and well being.

Digital change raised tech anxiety clearly. Autonomy lifted job satisfaction but dented well being, a mixed blessing. Work spilling into life hurt satisfaction and well being and fed burnout, while life spilling into work lifted satisfaction but cut engagement. Balanced hours helped both satisfaction and well being. Support for solo owners should target spillover and tech stress, not hours alone.
plos-pone-0350331:
Huipin Lin and co-authors improved a key estimate for electric car batteries in 2026: how much charge is left. Drivers and safety systems depend on that number, but it cannot be measured directly and shifts with use.

Their method pairs a neural network built for time series with a filtering method that smooths noisy output. Tested on three standard driving cycles from a university data set, it beat common rival networks on accuracy and stayed steady as conditions changed. Errors sat near one percent. Better charge estimates mean more honest range predictions and batteries managed with less guesswork.
plos-pone-0349231:
Hayley Reddington and co-authors compared two operations for a group of lung cancer patients in 2026: removing a whole lobe versus a smaller sublobar cut. Smaller surgery is tempting for small tumors, but its place after drug or radiation treatment given before surgery was unclear.

A national cancer database covering a decade yielded more than two thousand patients with small but node positive tumors treated before surgery. Under seven percent had the smaller operation. They left hospital sooner but had fewer lymph nodes checked. Survival comparisons followed. The rarity of the smaller cut after pre treatment itself signals surgical caution in this setting.
plos-pone-0350031:
Bryan S Hausman and co-authors used mice in 2026 to test whether shorter antibiotic courses protect the gut's resistance to invading germs. Broad antibiotics clear the gut microbes that normally block hospital pathogens, and course length is a lever doctors actually control.

Mice received a broad penicillin type drug for one, three, six, or ten days, then faced three dangerous gut invaders at set times after treatment. One day left resistance intact; longer courses broke it for periods that grew with course length. A narrower drug that spares gut anaerobes caused no break. The dose response gives prescribers concrete backing for shorter courses.
plos-pone-0349531:
Jiraporn Butta and colleagues tested doorstep delivery of HPV self sampling for cervical screening in rural Thailand in 2026. National coverage still misses world targets, and clinic based sampling forces women to travel during work hours.

Two villages were assigned to community delivery, with workshops and same day sample return, or to facility sampling with similar outreach. Women aged thirty to sixty were eligible. Uptake, feasibility, and acceptability were compared. Bringing the test to the village is the intervention, and the study measures its extra value inside a system already doing outreach, a fair and useful test.
plos-pone-0349931:
Phichpraorn Youngcharoen, Joachim G Voss, and co-authors studied what shapes how nurses manage pain in older patients who have trouble thinking clearly. Poor pain control in such patients is tied to anxiety, low mood, and worse quality of life, yet Thai evidence on the topic was thin. Their 2026 analysis reused questionnaire data from one hundred seventy-four full-time nurses who cared for these patients.

Statistical modeling explained over a third of the differences in nursing practice. Nurses who felt confident about pain care, and those who felt they worked well with doctors, managed pain better. Knowledge, experience, and teamwork also helped indirectly by building that confidence. The authors suggest training and workplace support aimed at confidence could improve pain care for a vulnerable group of patients.
plos-pone-0350131:
Ayalneh Demissie led a survey of school students in Asella, Ethiopia. The topic was violence between peers. The team asked what drives it at many levels. They used standard scales for behavior. They also gauged self-belief, or how well teens feel they can cope. More than five hundred students took part in 2026.

About forty-two in a hundred said peers had hurt them. About thirty-four in a hundred said they had hurt peers. Fifteen in a hundred were both bully and victim. That group had the lowest self-belief scores. Low self-belief was the strongest single sign of being a victim. The team urges schools to build teen confidence, not just police fights.
plos-pone-0349031:
Anna Carolina Nunes Ferraz, Lara Jansiski Motta, and co-authors published a 2026 protocol for a trial testing whether light therapy can ease the pain of intrauterine device placement in Brazil. The copper device is highly effective, yet only a small share of Brazilian women use it, and fear of insertion pain is a major reason. The planned study will randomly assign seventy-two women to real or sham light treatment, with neither patients nor assessors told which.

Pain will be scored at each step of insertion and at intervals over the following two days. The protocol also tracks painkiller use, anxiety, quality of life, satisfaction, and side effects. As a protocol, it reports no results: its purpose is to fix the design in public before the trial runs, so the eventual findings can be trusted.
plos-pone-0349631:
Serhii Nikulin and colleagues present a satellite method for tracking how farm landscapes change over time, tested on southern Ukraine, where war has damaged fields and irrigation systems. Their approach measures the outlines of landscape features, such as field borders, roads, and shelter belts, in images from the Sentinel-2 satellites. Broken or fading contours signal a degrading landscape.

A new contour density index turns the total length and contrast of these edges into numbers that can be compared across dates. Where fields fragment and boundaries vanish, the index drops. Such monitoring needs no one on the ground, which matters in areas that are dangerous to visit. It can help document war damage and plan farm recovery afterward.
plos-pone-0335831:
Mary Wandia Kivata and colleagues sequenced the gonorrhea bacterium from thirty-five patients across four regions of Kenya to chart which strains circulate and how they relate. Molecular surveillance of this infection is thin in Kenya, yet drug resistance in gonorrhea is a global emergency. Three typing schemes were applied to the same isolates, one of them designed specifically to track resistance.

The schemes found a wide spread of types, including many never recorded before: most of the fine-grained types were new to the databases. One established type appeared most often. A diverse, fast-changing strain pool complicates control, and a first detailed map like this gives Kenyan clinics and reference laboratories the baseline needed to spot resistant newcomers early.
plos-pone-0345231:
Maria Ishaq Khattak and a multinational team describe how they will judge the working parts of a community diabetes trial running in Pakistan and Afghanistan. The main trial, EMPOWER-D, uses participatory learning and action, where community groups meet, discuss, and act on local causes of type two diabetes. This protocol covers only the side study that watches the trial itself: how faithfully it is delivered, why it works or fails, and what local conditions shape it.

Checklists, attendance records, interviews, group discussions, and photo-based storytelling will feed the evaluation across three sites, guided by an official framework for such studies. No results are reported here. The authors say the lessons will show how to adapt and grow group-based prevention in places where health systems are stretched thin.
plos-pone-0346731:
Xiangyan Zhou and Xiaodong Liu study how task difficulty and personal anxiety together shape student translators' work. Translation students training from English face both harder texts and their own nerves. Their 2026 study has about one hundred Chinese learners each translate an easier and a harder passage, measuring working time, felt effort, revisions, and the quality of the result.

Harder tasks consistently changed performance across measures. Anxiety played a narrower role: it mainly altered how difficulty affected efficiency measures such as time and effort, rather than final quality. The pattern suggests nerves tax the process more than the product. Teachers might calm anxious students by pacing hard tasks and teaching coping routines, instead of only drilling language skill.
plos-pone-0347331:
Amr Ahmed Aly Ibrahim and co-workers search national survey data for what shapes breast self-examination among married women in Jordan. Breast cancer is the commonest cancer for Jordanian women, and self-checks aid early spotting. Their 2026 study analyzes the twenty twenty-three national family health survey, covering more than twelve thousand married women of childbearing age.

Only about one woman in five reported doing self-exams. Practice rose steeply with age, schooling, and wealth, and was higher among women who had borne several children. Media habits and place of residence also played parts. Campaigns aimed at younger, poorer, and less schooled women could close the widest gaps in this cheap early-warning habit.
plos-pone-0348631:
Elias dos Santos Batista and colleagues validated a wrist- and hip-worn movement tracker called ActTrust against laboratory measures of energy use. Devices like this let researchers estimate physical activity cheaply outside the lab, but each model needs its own calibration. In the 2026 study, fifty-six young adults walked and ran on a treadmill at four effort levels while breathing into a metabolic analyser.

Movement counts from the new device tracked treadmill speed and energy use almost as closely as the established comparison device. The team's conversion model sorted activities into intensity bands with good accuracy, especially at light and moderate effort. They conclude the cheaper device is fit for round-the-clock activity studies.
plos-pone-0347031:
Yue Jiang and colleagues mined a large Chinese health survey for a surprising clue to itchy, scaly skin rashes: the level of platelets in the blood. Dermatitis rashes are common and hard to tell apart from eczema or psoriasis. The team compared more than seven thousand people, of whom a small share had such rashes, looking for links that survive adjustment for other factors.

People with higher platelet counts were slightly less likely to have the rash, and the pattern held across several statistical models. The link was stronger in women. Past smoking and living in the countryside also tracked with the condition. The authors suggest platelet levels might one day sharpen risk prediction for this skin disorder.
plos-pone-0347531:
Shade J. Akinsete and colleagues surveyed one hundred sixty-two smallholder farmers in Nigeria's Ibarapa North district about how they handle pesticides. Most farmers knew pesticides harm health in principle, yet the 2026 study found knowledge and daily practice badly out of step. Only a small minority used goggles, two in five wore gloves, and skin contact during mixing and spraying was nearly universal.

Over half scored poorly on risk knowledge, and eighty-five percent had unsafe hygiene habits; the two failures reinforced each other. Empty containers were often dumped on the farm, and symptoms like dizziness, itchy eyes, and headaches were routine. The authors demand practical training and strict protective equipment use.
plos-pone-0347431:
Nobuyoshi Sugiyama and colleagues measured an enzyme's activity in the blood of Japanese children who faint or race when standing, a family of problems called orthostatic dysregulation. Its cause is unknown. Thirty young patients, most with the racing-heart subtype, were compared with healthy adults, testing how strongly the enzyme responded to adrenaline-like drugs.

The racing-heart group's enzyme activity ran significantly higher than both the delayed blood-pressure group and healthy adults, at every drug concentration tested. Their standing blood pressure also ran higher. The authors propose that an over-responsive enzyme helps drive the condition and could become a diagnostic marker distinguishing its subtypes.
plos-pone-0346231:
George Hancock, Innes Cuthill, and Jolyon Troscianko ran an online evolution experiment to ask how light and surroundings shape animal camouflage, reported in PLOS ONE in 2026. Real camouflage depends on weather, shadows, and the shape of the habitat, a mix too tangled to test easily on living animals, so the team evolved digital prey instead.

Under different lighting and habitat shapes, the artificial prey evolved different patterns, colors, and shading. Strong versus soft light changed how bold the internal patterning became, and geometry altered the shapes that worked best. The results also showed that common measures of camouflage quality shift with conditions, a warning for field studies that ignore lighting.
plos-pone-0347931:
Melissa Clarkson, Noah Perry, and Landon Detwiler introduce a formal vocabulary for describing pictures so computers can work with them, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Images normally hold meaning only for human eyes; their Graphic Descriptor Ontology gives graphics and their parts structured labels, drawing on ideas from art, semiotics, and technical communication.

The system treats a graphic as an arrangement of three kinds of marks: lines, points, and regions, each with roles and qualities that can be annotated. The authors apply it to libraries of anatomical standard drawings, where consistent labeling matters for teaching and reference. A shared scheme of this kind could let software search, compare, and explain images rather than merely store them.
plos-pone-0348231:
Xiaodan Pu and colleagues adapt a rapid DNA test for shrimp farms in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. The target is Vibrio parahaemolyticus, a bacterium that sickens shrimp and people, and the usual test needs DNA extracted in a lab, which is slow on a farm. Their version skips extraction: boiled pond water goes straight into the reaction.

They challenged the test with water from eight whiteleg shrimp systems spanning wide ranges of salt, acidity, and dirt loads. Most water conditions barely mattered, but high salinity dulled the test's sensitivity, a limit farmers should know. A pond-side test that works in minutes could help growers catch outbreaks before they wipe out a crop.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
A year of Cyprus renewals closed with one more in December 1966. On the fifteenth, the Council adopted Resolution 231 without dissent. The Secretary-General's report held that the force was still needed to keep peace. The Cyprus government agreed it should stay past late December.

The text restates the long list of earlier Cyprus decisions. It urges all parties to show the utmost restraint. It also asks them to keep working together toward the Council's goals. The posting then runs on for a further period. By late 1966, the pattern was fixed. The force could neither solve the Cyprus problem nor leave it.

Mediation, not troops, was the Council's offer in the Indonesia dispute of 1947. On 25 August, it adopted Resolution 31. Eight members voted yes and none voted no. Three members held back from the vote. Three weeks before, Resolution 27 had called for a halt to the fighting.

The Council now tenders its good offices to both sides. It offers help through a panel of three Council members. Each party would pick one member of the panel. Those two would then choose the third. The offer grew into the Committee of Good Offices. That body walked with Indonesia toward full independence in 1949.

Guinea's break with France brought its bid to the Council within weeks in 1958. On 9 December, it adopted Resolution 131. Guinea had voted that autumn for instant freedom in a referendum. It was the only French colony to choose that path in 1958. A republic was proclaimed at once under its new leaders.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit the Republic of Guinea. Admission followed days later. Guinea's arrival marked an early sign of the wave to come. African decolonization would reshape the UN's ranks and its politics within a few short years.

An odd, precise span marks this Iran-Iraq observer renewal of 1989. On 8 February, the Council adopted Resolution 631. The observer group had watched the truce line since August 1988. The peace text behind it, Resolution 598, was still not carried out. The Secretary-General's February report grounded the step.

The text calls once again on the parties to act on Resolution 598 at once. It renews the mandate for seven months and twenty-two days. The term ends on 30 September 1989. A report on the state of play is due from the Secretary-General then. The odd end date matched the UN planning calendar, not a round half-year.

Cyprus, again, is the real subject of Resolution 1331. Some digests mislabel it as a Golan Heights text. In fact it was adopted unanimously on 13 December 2000, after the Secretary-General's report on the Cyprus operation. UNFICYP peacekeepers had guarded the island's buffer zone for decades.

The Council extended UNFICYP's mandate to 15 June 2001. It asked for an implementation report by 1 June. It also pressed the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces on a sore point. Restrictions imposed in June 2000 had hampered the peacekeepers. Members demanded those limits be lifted. They wanted the former military position restored at Strovilia, a village inside the buffer zone.

Resolution 1531, adopted unanimously on 12 March 2004, voices frustration at a peace process stuck between Ethiopia and Eritrea. The boundary commission had reported in February that it could not move ahead with marking the border under present conditions. The Council blamed the impasse mainly on missing progress in demarcation, and singled out Ethiopia's refusal to accept key parts of the binding ruling, and its weak cooperation.

The Council kept UNMEE, the UN mission in both countries, in place for a further six months. It restated support for the Algiers Agreements and the commission's 2002 ruling, which both sides had accepted as final. The text warned, in effect, that a peace both governments had signed was being undone by delay.

Resolution 431, adopted on 27 July 1978, puts a negotiator in charge of Namibia's road to independence. A settlement proposal for the territory, prepared by five Western governments and circulated that April, was on the table. The Council's 1976 resolution had already laid down the goal: a free Namibia, chosen by its own people.

The Council asked the UN chief to name a special envoy for Namibia. His task was to make sure independence came early, through free elections under UN supervision and control. The Secretary-General also had to report back as soon as possible with recommendations for carrying out the proposal. The appointment set up the UN operation that, after long delays, finally ran Namibia's founding election in 1989.

Resolution 1831, passed on 19 August 2008, keeps the African force in Somalia for six more months. The force, AMISOM, was small and based in Mogadishu. It worked in the midst of a fierce revolt. The Council condemned bids to block peace talks by force. It deplored fresh calls to arms and fresh attacks on aid staff and peace staff alike.

The force won six more months of cover from the Council. Calm in Somalia, the text says, needs arms laid down and ex-fighters brought back to civil life. The Council restated its respect for the land's unity and its borders. It also wove this grant into its web of past texts on guards for the weak, for children, and for aid teams.

How the UN should work with regional bodies on peace and security is the theme of Resolution 1631, adopted on 17 October 2005. It rests on Chapter VIII of the UN Charter, which covers regional arrangements. The 2005 World Summit had urged a bigger role for regional groups, and a new Peacebuilding Commission was about to be created.

The Council invites regional and subregional groups with peacekeeping skill to place that strength in the UN Standby Arrangements System. It urges states to help build up such groups, above all in Africa, with people, training, and money. It stresses fast deployment in support of UN missions and the role of regional groups against the illegal small arms trade and terrorism. It also plans regular meetings with regional heads and asks for a report on the chances and problems in this teamwork.

Resolution 1931, adopted on 29 June 2010, deals with the judges and timetable of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. The tribunal had been told to finish its work in 2010, but its own report said that goal could not be met. Skilled staff were leaving, and a string of trials and appeals still had years to run.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the terms of the appeals judges until 31 December 2012 and of the trial judges until 31 December 2011, or until their cases end. It lets nine short-term ad litem judges serve past the usual three-year limit. It presses states, above all those of the former Yugoslavia, to help the tribunal and arrest those still indicted. It also urges the tribunal to finish its work as fast as it can.

The Dayton peace deal for Bosnia and Herzegovina is put into force by Resolution 1031, adopted on 15 December 1995. The General Framework Agreement had been signed in Paris the day before by Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. A London conference had set up a Peace Implementation Council to guide the work ahead.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes a multinational implementation force, IFOR, under unified command, with power to use all needed measures to enforce the military parts of the deal. It ends UNPROFOR's mandate once authority passes to IFOR. It backs elections run by the OSCE, the right of refugees to go home, and full cooperation with the war crimes tribunal. It also endorses a High Representative to oversee the civilian side of the settlement, agreeing to the designation named in the text.

Liberia's sanctions are renewed in Resolution 1731, adopted on 20 December 2006. The new government had made real progress since January 2006, passing a forestry reform law, and the timber measures had already been lifted. Diamond controls were not yet in place, though work toward the Kimberley Process was under way. The expert panel found that the conditions for ending the remaining measures were not yet met.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo and travel ban for 12 months, with an exemption for non-lethal equipment for vetted, trained Liberian police and security forces. It renews the rough-diamond ban for six months, with a review after four, to give Liberia time to build a transparent certificate-of-origin regime. The asset freeze from Resolution 1532 stays in force. The Panel of Experts is extended to 20 June 2007, reporting by 6 June 2007.

Sierra Leone's observer mission is extended and sent back to the capital in Resolution 1231, adopted on 11 March 1999. The situation remained fragile after the recent escalation of violence. The Secretary-General's fifth report of 4 March 1999 recommended the move. Reports persisted that rebels were receiving arms and mercenaries, in particular from Liberian territory.

The Council extends the mandate of the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, UNOMSIL, until 13 June 1999. It welcomes the plan to re-establish UNOMSIL in Freetown as soon as possible with more military observers and human rights personnel, subject to strict attention to security. It condemns rebel atrocities against civilians, especially women and children, including recruiting children as soldiers, and demands full humanitarian access. It reaffirms the Resolution 1171 (1998) arms embargo, commends ECOMOG, and asks the Secretary-General to report by 5 June 1999 with recommendations on UNOMSIL's future deployment.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: On 9 February 1946, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 31. It was adopted at the twenty-sixth plenary meeting of the first session. It is a single short instruction. The Assembly told the Secretary-General to put one question on the agenda of the second part of that first session. The question was whether to hold an international press conference. The choice itself was left for later debate.

General Assembly Resolution 2231 (XXI), from the twenty-first session in 1966, returned to the question of Gibraltar a year after resolution 2070 (XX) had urged talks. The Assembly noted that Spain and the United Kingdom, the ruling power, both said they were willing to keep negotiating. But it regretted acts that had harmed the talks.

The text voiced regret at the delay in ending colonial rule in Gibraltar under the 1960 declaration. Both parties were called on to press on with their talks. They were to keep in mind the interests of the territory's people. Britain was asked to speed the process and report back before the next session.

General Assembly resolution 69/31 (2014) concerns preventing an arms race in outer space. The Assembly reaffirms that space exploration must serve peaceful purposes under the Outer Space Treaty. It reaffirms that the existing legal regime alone does not guarantee against an arms race there. It calls on all states, especially major space powers, to work toward that goal and refrain from contrary actions. It invites the Conference on Disarmament to set up a working group on the subject during its 2015 session. The group would pursue negotiated agreements, including verification measures.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Short-term judges come to the Rwanda war crimes tribunal in this text of 14 August 2002. The tribunal's president had asked for the change so trials could finish sooner. A similar ad litem system already existed at the tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council amended the Rwanda tribunal's Statute to create the pool, and adjusted related articles of the Yugoslavia tribunal's Statute too. The Secretary-General is asked to arrange the election of 18 ad litem judges for Rwanda as soon as possible. Staff and facilities for the new judges were to follow, so the extra courtroom capacity could actually be used.

The Central African Republic had held elections in 2011, but armed groups still controlled much of the country outside the capital. One of them, the Lord's Resistance Army, crossed borders to raid villages. Resolution 2031, adopted on 21 December 2011, concerns BINUCA, the United Nations peacebuilding office in the country.

The Council extended BINUCA's mandate until 31 January 2013. It pushed the government to set up a permanent, independent body to run future elections. The electoral code also had to be revised. The office would keep backing the peace agreement process and disarmament work. Regional efforts against the Lord's Resistance Army received support as well. The aim was to help the state extend its authority beyond the capital.

Egypt's foreign minister addressed the Council on the Middle East in April 1973, and Resolution 331 followed on 20 April. The short text asks the Secretary-General for a full report. The report had to cover every effort the United Nations had made on the Middle East situation since June 1967. It was to reach the Council as early as possible. Once the report arrived, the Council would meet to examine the situation. The Secretary-General's special envoy for the region was to be on hand to assist during that debate.
un-sc-res-231:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force came up for renewal again in December 1966. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 8 December, said the force was still needed if peace was to be maintained. Cyprus's government agreed it should stay beyond 26 December. Resolution 231 was adopted unanimously on 15 December 1966.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, reaching back to Resolution 186 of 1964. The parties were urged to show the utmost restraint. They were also told to keep working together toward the Council's goals. The force's stationing was extended for six months, ending on 26 June 1967. The Council hoped that enough progress toward a settlement would be made by then. Such progress might at last allow the force to leave the island.
un-sc-res-31:
Indonesia's fight for independence from the Netherlands brought the Council back to the dispute in August 1947. Resolution 27, passed on 1 August, had called on both sides to stop fighting. It had also pointed them toward a peaceful settlement. One part of that text let the parties ask for the Council's help. Resolution 31, adopted on 25 August 1947, makes that offer in form.

The Council resolved to tender its good offices to the parties. In plain terms, it offered its own help to bring about a peaceful settlement of the dispute. If the parties asked, the help would come through a small committee of the Council. The committee would have three members. Each party would choose one member, and the two chosen would name the third. The offer put the Council's mediation on the table, ready for the Dutch and the Republic of Indonesia to use.
un-sc-res-631:
United Nations observers were watching the Iran-Iraq ceasefire in early 1989. On 8 February 1989 the Security Council renewed their mission, UNIIMOG. The Secretary-General had reported on the observer group two days before. The Council took note of his observations. It also recalled resolution 598, the text that had demanded an end to the war.

The renewal ran for seven months and twenty-two days. It ended on 30 September 1989. The Council called on both parties to carry out resolution 598 without delay. The Secretary-General owed a report at the end of the period. It would cover events on the ground and steps taken toward a settlement.
un-sc-res-1531:
Ethiopia and Eritrea's stalled border process framed a mission renewal on 12 March 2004. The Boundary Commission's twelfth report, of 27 February 2004, said it could not move forward with demarcation as things stood. Ethiopia rejected large parts of the commission's binding ruling and was not cooperating. Eritrea refused to deal with the Secretary-General's special envoy.

The Council extended the United Nations Mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, UNMEE, at its set troop and observer levels to 15 September 2004. It urged both parties to cooperate fully and quickly with the mission and to guard its staff. Final duty for applying the Algiers Agreements and the boundary ruling rested with the two governments, the Council stressed. It backed the special envoy's good offices and pressed both sides to open a direct air route between Asmara and Addis Ababa. Delays, it noted, were raising the mission's costs.
un-sc-res-431:
Namibia's path to a United Nations settlement plan advanced on 27 July 1978. The Council recalled resolution 385 (1976), which had demanded free elections for the territory. A proposal for a settlement of the Namibian situation had been laid before it on 10 April 1978, in document S/12636. The Western contact group's plan was now on the table.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to appoint a special representative for Namibia. His task was to secure the territory's early independence through free elections under United Nations supervision and control. The Secretary-General also had to report at the earliest date with advice on putting the settlement proposal into effect under resolution 385. All concerned were urged to do their best to bring Namibia to independence as soon as possible. The special representative's work became the core of the settlement effort the Council pursued from that summer on.
un-sc-res-1831:
AMISOM's authorization was renewed on 19 August 2008. The African Union had already extended its Somalia mission from 17 July 2008 for six more months. Uganda and Burundi kept troops in Mogadishu. The Council condemned all violence inside Somalia and acts meant to block a peaceful political process. It stressed the need for disarmament and reintegration of fighters.

The Council renewed the authorization of African Union member states to run AMISOM for a further six months. The mission could take all necessary measures to carry out its mandate under resolution 1744 (2007). The arms embargo terms of resolution 733 (1992) would not block supplies meant for the mission. African Union states were urged to send more troops, and all member states were asked for money, staff, and equipment. The Secretary-General was encouraged to keep working with the African Union on plans for a possible United Nations force to follow.
un-sc-res-1631:
Cooperation with regional bodies was set out as doctrine on 17 October 2005. Chapter VIII of the Charter supplied the legal frame. The 2005 World Summit outcome had just been adopted. The sixth high-level meeting with regional organizations had closed in July. The Council recalled its own debates of 2003 and 2004 on working with regional partners.

The Council voiced its resolve to deepen cooperation with regional and subregional organizations. All states and bodies were urged to give money and skills to build their capacity, above all in Africa. Regional strategies inside the United Nations system had to grow. The Council stressed what regional bodies can do in settling disputes, peacekeeping, and rebuilding after war. It meant to hold regular meetings with the heads of regional organizations. Its own committees were praised for drawing such partners into the fight against terrorism and arms spread.
un-sc-res-1931:
Yugoslav tribunal judges had their terms stretched again on 29 June 2010. The tribunal's president had written on 31 May about the bench. Its completion strategy report admitted the work would not end in 2010, as ordered. The loss of experienced staff was slowing the trials. Resolution 1900 (2009) had promised a review by this date.

The Council restated that persons indicted by the tribunal must face trial. It noted the need for the tribunal to be staffed well enough to finish. The terms of the permanent trial judges were extended to 31 December 2011, or to the end of their cases if sooner. Appeals judges' terms ran on in the same way, to the dates set out in the text. Ad litem judges gained matching extensions. Named ad litem judges were allowed to sit past their terms to finish the cases before them.
un-sc-res-1031:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 1031 put the Dayton peace agreement for Bosnia into force. The Council adopted it on 15 December 1995, one day after the agreement was signed in Paris. The war in Bosnia had killed many thousands and driven many more from their homes.

The text welcomes the peace deal and calls on all sides to keep their promises. It lets member states set up a NATO-led force, called IFOR, to guard the deal. That force could use all needed means to make the parties obey. The Council also backs a High Representative to watch over the civilian side of the peace.
un-sc-res-1731:
Liberia sanctions are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1731, adopted on 20 December 2006. Liberia's new elected government had made real gains since January 2006. A new forestry law had passed, and the ban on timber exports had been lifted. Yet the Council judged that other reforms still fell short.

The text renews the arms and travel bans for twelve more months. The ban on rough diamond exports runs six more months, with a review after four. Liberia must build a clear origin scheme for its diamonds and join the Kimberley Process. The expert panel that checks the sanctions stays on until 20 June 2007.
un-sc-res-1231:
Resolution 1231 on Sierra Leone was adopted on 11 March 1999. Rebels had attacked the capital that January and committed grave atrocities against civilians. Most United Nations observers had pulled out to Conakry for safety. Reports kept saying arms and fighters reached the rebels through Liberia.

The Council extends the observer mission, called UNOMSIL, until 13 June 1999. The mission should move back into Freetown as soon as safety allows. More military observers and human rights staff will join it. The text condemns rebel abuse of women and children and the use of child soldiers. All states must honor the arms embargo on rebel forces.
un-sc-res-1331:
Council members took up Cyprus and unanimously adopted Resolution 1331 on Cyprus on 13 December 2000. The peacekeeping force on the island had served since 1964. Cyprus had agreed the force should stay past mid-December. New limits placed on its patrols that June had raised concern.

The Council extends the force, called UNFICYP, until 15 June 2001. It urges the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to lift the limits set on 30 June 2000. The old military position at Strovilia should be restored. The text also backs urgent work on the fate of missing persons. A fresh report is due by 1 June 2001.
europmc-pmc10161731:
Ruze and colleagues review the links between obesity and type 2 diabetes in a 2023 paper, covering spread, causes, and treatment. Both conditions have grown steadily more common across the world. They share genetic and lifestyle roots, and excess weight strongly raises the chance that diabetes will develop.

The review explains how stored fat, especially around inner organs, disrupts sugar control. It surveys treatments that address both conditions at once, from lifestyle change to surgery. The authors make the case for treating the pair as one problem. They argue that joint care gives better results.
europmc-pmc10172131:
Schneider, Lee, and Mathis present a method for analyzing animal behavior and brain activity together, in a 2023 study. Linking what an animal does to what its neurons do is a core goal of neuroscience. As recordings grow larger, scientists need models that can find shared patterns across both kinds of data.

Their method learns compact embeddings, or summaries, that capture behavior and neural signals in one frame. It can then relate movements to brain states in fine detail. The tool, called CEBRA, opens new ways to study how brains produce adaptive behavior.
europmc-pmc10439131:
Arora and colleagues mapped two zones of mouth tumours in 2023 and linked them to patient outcomes. The cancer is oral squamous cell carcinoma not tied to the HPV virus. The team read gene activity in single cells and in tissue, keeping each cell's place. They set the tumour core against its leading edge, the rim that pushes outward.

Each zone had its own gene profile and its own mix of nearby cells. The edge profile was much the same across many cancer types, while the core was tissue-specific. Arora found that a strong edge mark tied to worse survival in many cancers. The core mark tied to better outcomes. A model of cell growth in place also foretold drug response.
europmc-pmc10635831:
Blanco-Míguez and co-authors released MetaPhlAn 4 in 2023, a tool to name microbes in a sample. The tool reads DNA from a whole community at once, a method called metagenomics. Past versions could name only species in a fixed catalogue. Many real species have never been grown or named.

The new version draws on 1.01 million microbe genomes, from lab strains and sample builds. Blanco-Míguez defines marker genes for 26,970 species-level groups. Of those, 4,992 have no species name yet. The tool explains about 20% more of the DNA in human gut samples than before. In farm animal guts the gain passed 40%. It can even track single strains of unnamed species.
europmc-pmc10700131:
Merchant and co-authors scaled deep learning in 2023 to find new stable materials. New crystals drive gains from chips to batteries, yet trial-and-error hunts are slow and costly. The team trained graph networks, AI that learns from atom links, on a far larger scale than past work. Their base held 48,000 known stable crystals.

The models flagged 2.2 million new structures as stable, an order-of-magnitude leap. Merchant reports that 736 of them had in fact been made in labs on their own. Top finds will be shared for screening toward uses such as layered materials and battery electrolytes. The same scale yielded atom force models of high accuracy for later studies.
europmc-pmc1084331:
Hippenmeyer and co-authors probe timing in nerve growth in this 2005 mouse study. Dorsal root ganglion neurons are nerve cells that carry touch and body signals to the spine. Two gene switches, called ETS factors, switch on late in their growth under signals from their targets. These switches guide late steps such as reaching the target and branching.

The team forced the switches on too early in young nerve cells. Early switching warped the wires' paths and blocked the cells from gaining their final traits, they found. It also changed how much the cells leaned on growth support factors. The authors conclude that nerve cells pass through a timed switch in how they answer these signals. Getting the timing right, they say, is part of normal nerve wiring.
europmc-pmc11446831:
Schlegel and a large team annotate every neuron class in the fruit fly brain in this 2024 paper. The FlyWire project had mapped the wiring of about 140,000 neurons in the fly brain. Wiring alone does not say what each cell is. The team added a systematic annotation, in a hierarchy, of cell types, neuronal classes, and developmental lineages.

The count came to 8,453 cell types. Of these, 3,643 matched types proposed in an earlier partial map, they report. Another 4,581 are new, mostly from regions the earlier map lacked. About one third of the earlier types could not be reliably reidentified, despite matching cell shapes. The authors therefore propose a new definition: a cell type must be more similar across two brains than to any other cell within the same brain. They validate it by jointly analysing both connectomes.
europmc-pmc1183531:
Hansen and colleagues screened the roundworm C. elegans for long life genes in 2005. Most aging knowledge came from mutants found for other reasons. That history could bias what scientists think aging is. A full genome screen offered a fairer test.

The screen found 23 new genes that extend worm lifespan. They touch signals, stress defense, gene control, and metabolism. Eating less seemed to work by quieting certain key genes. Hansen also flags a hormone path tied to a known aging switch. Nearly all new genes fit known paths, which supports past work.
europmc-pmc1280331:
Delfino, Sioutas, and Malik weighed ultrafine particles in heart harm from air pollution in 2005. Daily studies link particle mass to heart admissions and deaths. Panel studies add links to ischemia, blood pressure, and rhythm changes. The exact causal component stayed unidentified.

Ultrafine particles under 0.1 micrometers dominate particle counts and surface area. That surface can carry large loads of toxic pollutants. Combustion products show up in the indirect evidence so far. The authors argue reactive cargo in ultrafines reaches heart targets. Fossil fuel combustion sits at the center of their case. Panel data back the time trend data well.
europmc-pmc1464831:
Even mice with the same genes gain weight in unlike ways on a rich diet. Koza and co-authors used that spread in 2006 to hunt for non-gene drivers of obesity. Male mice on a high-fat diet showed a four-fold spread in body fat. High and low gainers could be told apart at six weeks, before the rich diet began.

Fat samples taken at seven weeks showed gene activity gaps that foretold later fat gain. Genes in the Wnt signal path and tissue reshaping stood out. Koza points to one Wnt blocker, SFRP5, among others. The team proposes that fat tissue holds marks that set obesity risk.
europmc-pmc1750931:
HIV builds its new particles at the cell's outer skin, not in inner compartments. Jouvenet and co-authors settled that debate in 2006. Prevailing models held that assembly starts on late endosomes, inner membrane sacs, and rides outward.

Blocking endosome movement did not stop the viral protein Gag reaching the surface or virions being released. Targeting assembly to the surface worked; targeting it to endosomes did not. Gag first gathered at the surface, and the share later seen inside had been swallowed back. Jouvenet concludes assembly begins and completes at the plasma membrane.
europmc-pmc1808431: Multiple-color optical activation, silencing, and desynchronization of neural activity, with single-spike temporal resolution. — a 2005 science paper on multicolor brain control. It flips brain cells on and off for labs. The paper is the brain-flip study: the notes on cell control, filed here in full session today.

europmc-pmc2002031: Alcohol, physical activity and other risk factors for colorectal cancer: a prospective study. — a 2005 science paper on booze, exercise and colon cancer. It studies the risk factors. The paper is the risk-factor study: the findings on colorectal ills, filed here in session.
