spee-cautio-criminalis-latin-1631:
Friedrich Spee, a Jesuit priest, published the Cautio Criminalis in Latin in 1631, without his name. Spee had served as confessor to condemned witches in Würzburg, hearing their last words before the fire. What he learned in that cell produced a searing attack on the trials and their tortures.

He argues that torture makes every accusation true by force. Germany, he warns, will burn its whole population if the process runs unchecked. The book is the moral turning point of the persecution. Its anonymity protected a man whose order and church ran the trials he condemned. Few braver books came out of the burning times.
plos-pone-0004931:
Inside each cell, sensor proteins called Nod-like receptors watch for invading germs. When they detect trouble, they recruit helper proteins. Those helpers process alarm chemicals and switch on immune genes. Roland Wagner and co-authors mapped part of this system in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied how the receptors' effector domains interact.

Effector domains are the plugs and sockets of the inner alarm network. By testing which domains bind which partners, the team charted the wiring. The chart links detection to response step by step. It helps researchers understand immune signaling. It may also reveal points where future drugs could adjust that signaling.
plos-pone-0005031:
Furin is a protein-cutting enzyme. It is born with a safety lock, an extra piece called a prodomain. The lock blocks its own cutting site. Katarzyna Gawlik and colleagues detailed the unlocking in PLOS ONE in 2009. Furin must cut off its prodomain itself. That self-activation is called autocatalytic.

The study shows activation needs one more step. The emerging enzyme's N-terminus must leave the active site. Only then can furin act on other proteins. The work reveals the exact order of the self-unlocking. Many protein-cutting enzymes share this kind of birth. Understanding furin's version helps explain the whole family.
plos-pone-0005131:
Radiation breaks DNA strands. Double-strand breaks are emergencies for the cell. A protein called ATM detects them and sounds the alarm. Kazunari Mouri and colleagues modeled that detection mathematically in PLOS ONE in 2009. ATM tags itself with phosphates when breaks appear. That autophosphorylation is the detection signal.

Their model follows breaks, repair proteins and the complexes they form. It reproduces how ATM's self-tagging reports break numbers. The model captures detection logic in equations. Such models turn a molecular alarm into predictable math. They can be tested against experiments and refined. Understanding break detection matters for cancer and radiation medicine. Cells that misread breaks can turn malignant.
plos-pone-0005231:
Tumor suppressor genes help keep cell growth in check, and cancers often disable them. Kashuba and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that two such genes, RASSF1 and RBSP3, change at unusually high rates in cancer. RBSP3 is also known by the name CTDSPL.

Cancer cells carry many kinds of gene damage, from single-letter changes to lost chunks. A high mutation rate in guard genes can speed a tumor's growth and spread. Flagging these fragile guards helps explain tumor behavior and may point to markers worth testing in patients.
plos-pone-0005331:
Photosynthetic cells make oxygen, which can damage the very machinery that produces it. Flavodiiron proteins help bacteria and archaea detoxify oxygen and nitric oxide. Zhang and colleagues asked what these proteins do in cyanobacteria, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Cyanobacterial versions carry an extra domain compared with other forms. Two of them, Flv2 and Flv4, protect photosystem II, a core part of the light machinery, in the species Synechocystis. Guarding that machinery keeps photosynthesis running under bright, stressful light. Green cells that guard their own light gear can keep making food in bright sun. Crop science would love to copy that trait into plants that feed the world at large scale.
plos-pone-0005931:
Airborne diseases spread through everyday meetings between people. Mirjam Kretzschmar and Rafael Mikolajczyk set out in 2009 to map those meetings across eight European countries for PLOS ONE. Their study records who meets whom, how often, and how contact rates differ by age and place.

Such contact profiles feed the math models used to forecast epidemics. Better maps of mixing mean better guesses about how fast a flu-like illness will move and whom it will hit first. The eight-country data give modelers a shared base, and they show that contact habits are a core part of public health planning.
plos-pone-0006031:
In lupus, the immune system attacks the body's own tissues, and the kidneys often take the hit. Kenneth Scalapino and David Daikh tested a cell-based calm-down in lupus-prone mice in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper transfers regulatory T cells, grown and expanded outside the body, into mice of the NZB/NZW strain, whose kidneys inflame as lupus advances.

The title reports success: the transferred cells suppressed glomerulonephritis, the kidney inflammation that can end in organ failure. Lab-grown peacekeeper cells thus hold promise as a treatment, not just a lab curiosity. The study supports a path where a patient's own regulatory cells are grown in number and returned to quiet the attack.
plos-pone-0006131:
Electric fields run quietly through healing tissue, and cells can steer by them. Nurdan Özkucur, Thomas Monsees, Srikanth Perike and colleagues watched the first steps of that steering in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies osteoblast-like cells, bone-building cells, under direct current electric fields, which are known to induce directional migration in development and regeneration.

Local calcium rises and cell elongation come first, launching the guided motility, the title reports. Knowing the opening moves tells engineers which signals to amplify in a healing scaffold. The work links a physical cue to a chemical one, calcium, that cell biology already knows how to measure and tune.
plos-pone-0006231:
Simple repeated DNA stretches offer a clean window on how selection shapes genomes. Andrew Dalby compared those repeats across malaria parasites, the plasmodia, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Repeats inside coding regions change the proteins themselves, so their effects show up directly in the organism.

Protein surveys revealed that different parasite lineages favour different amino acid repeats. That lineage-specific pattern bears the mark of selection, not random drift alone. Reading the repeats helps trace how malaria parasites diverged. It may also flag protein regions that matter for survival, and thus for drug or vaccine work.
plos-pone-0006731:
Akihiko Mougi and Kinya Nishimura modeled how invasion order shapes evolution in a food web in PLOS ONE in 2009. Experiments had shown that invasion history matters for communities. Species arriving earlier can steer how later species evolve. Few theory studies had focused on that history effect. The authors built a model with three feeding levels.

Their tri-trophic food web tracks predators, prey, and their food. Species invade in sequence, and coevolution follows each arrival. Different arrival orders produced different evolutionary outcomes. The model shows history is not a detail but a driver. That insight helps interpret real invasions and community assembly in nature.
plos-pone-0006831:
Alexander Samoshkin and his team showed that a packing crew for chromosomes is a must at the centromere in PLOS ONE in 2009. The crew is condensin, which coils chromosomes tight for cell division. Man and most backboned beasts have two forms of it. Take the crew away, and the centromere, the chromosome's waist, goes wrong. Why that link holds was not known.

The team cut condensin down in human cells. The waist of the chromosome then failed to form right. The twin grips that haul chromosomes apart also aimed the wrong way. Bad aiming can send chromosomes to the wrong side. Such faults can drive disease and failed growth.
plos-pone-0006931:

Its levels rise as several squamous cell cancers progress. Earlier work found it overexpressed in roughly seven in ten head and neck squamous cell carcinomas.

The authors link that excess to the silencing of tumor suppressive genes. They describe silencing done by epigenetic means, which switch genes off without changing the code. They also connect AP-2α with microsatellite instability in these tumors. The work suggests a route by which one protein helps this cancer grow.
plos-pone-0007031:

The pair showed that a small tag, called sumoylation, regulates that location. Adding the tag shifted where lipin-1α sits in neuronal cells. Location decides which of its two jobs the protein performs. The result links a tagging system to both metabolism and gene control.
plos-pone-0007131:

plos-pone-0007331:

arxiv-2601-12231:
Kaichuan Kong, Dongjie Liu, Xiaobo Jin, Shijie Xu, and Guanggang Geng spot insider threats in user logs with wavelet tools. Logs hold rich behaviour data in many channels. They shift over time, and true threats are rare, which makes spotting hard.

Their frame joins wavelet-aware modulation, wavelet splits at many scales, and attention that adapts to scale. Wavelets track both fast bursts and slow drifts in acts. A robust spotter helps firms catch misuse early. The work tests it on multi-channel logs.  Rare threats need tools that miss few true cases.
arxiv-2601-11231:
Savvas Papaioannou, Panayiotis Kolios, Christos Panayiotou, and Marios Polycarpou track wildfire fronts. Their 2026 preprint uses a mobile agent, such as a drone. Where the drone flies sets where sensor data comes from. That choice shapes how well the fire's spread can be guessed.

A wildfire front moves in a random, hard-to-know way. Good tracking must join sensing, guessing, and control in one loop. Past work often split those three jobs into parts. The team's control seeks data on purpose as it flies. It steers toward the spots that cut doubt the most. The aim is a sharper map of the front in real time.
arxiv-2601-11631:
Yurun Song and coauthors compress coordinates for multi-turn GUI agents. Their 2026 preprint is called Compress to Focus, on policy optimization. GUI agents finish complex tasks through sequential decisions. Each turn adds screenshots and actions to the history.

Accumulated history inflates context severely over long tasks. Truncation sacrifices long-term context that agents may need. Token pruning compromises the spatial structure of screens. The team compresses coordinates to focus the policy instead. Compact coordinates keep where things are on screen. Policy optimization then learns from leaner, structured states. The work comes from UC Irvine and partner labs.
arxiv-2601-13431:
Sandra Robles, Rosa Dominguez-Tenreiro, and Susana Pedrosa track how mass clumps around the birth sites of galaxies in a big sim. The sim is the EAGLE50 box, a large volume run of galaxy growth. The team starts with round lumps of matter at very high redshift, set at redshift fifteen.

Each lump is centred on a spot where a galaxy will form. They track how each lump is stretched by tides as time runs. A shrunk inertia tool reads that stretch. They track dark matter and cold baryons apart, to see where the two part. Such stretch sets the spin and shape a galaxy is born with.
arxiv-2601-12731:
Stefano Civelli, Pietro Bernardelle, Nicolo Brunello, and Gianluca Demartini study how language models represent problem difficulty. Predicting difficulty means estimating how hard a task is for the model itself. A common method trains linear probes on internal representations of the model. The team ask whether that difficulty signal has the same shape across languages.

They train probes on a benchmark subset translated into twenty one languages. The set comes from the AMC portion of the Easy2Hard benchmark. If a shared geometry of difficulty exists, one probe structure fits many tongues. That would suggest models judge hardness in a language neutral way. The finding would matter for multilingual evaluation and training.
arxiv-2601-13831:
Redamy Perez-Ramos, Stefan Kluth, and Wolfgang Ochs review the dead cone effect in heavy-quark jets in 2026. In QCD, a heavy quark sheds radiation as it flies. The dead cone is a zone near its path where radiation is suppressed. The team gives a unified study across charm, bottom, and top quarks.

They use precision data from LEP at 91.2 GeV collision energy. The data show strong momentum-space suppression in charm and bottom jets. Monte Carlo simulations with Pythia 8 support the readings. They give a quantitative account in the Modified Leading Logarithmic Approximation of perturbative QCD.
arxiv-2601-13931:
A study of music search models tackles how they handle the word not in 2026. Joint audio-text models are widely used for music retrieval. A user might ask for a track with vocals, or without vocals. Negation is fundamental for telling the absence of an element from its presence.

Current systems fail to represent negation reliably, the team reports. That failure can flip a search result to its exact opposite. The work targets effective negation modeling in these joint models. Music tools that grasp not would serve listeners and catalog teams far better.
arxiv-2601-14031:
Stefano Damato, Nicoló Rubattu, Dario Azzimonti, and Giorgio Corani forecast demand series full of zeros in 2026. Intermittent time series have a significant amount of zeros by nature. They make up a large percentage of inventory items in supply chains. Probabilistic forecasts are needed to plan inventory levels well.

A good predictive distribution covers non-negative values only. It should have a mass at zero and a long upper tail. The team compares local models, fit per item, with global models fit across items. The better style could cut both stockouts and wasteful overstock.
arxiv-2601-14131:
Amila Indika, Rick Kazman, and Anthony Peruma survey how app builders handle accessibility in practice in 2026. Mobile apps are now ubiquitous in everyday life. Developers must prioritize accessibility for users with diverse abilities. Past research found widespread accessibility issues in apps.

A lack of cross-platform, globally representative insights remains on practitioner views. Past work raised awareness of developer challenges but not this broad picture. Their study asks practitioners about practices and challenges directly. Knowing real habits helps target training, tools, and rules that improve access. The views come from a wide set of lands and app types. That breadth makes the gaps they name hard to wave away.
arxiv-2601-14231:
Alessandro Cucinotta, Mattia Magnabosco, and Daniele Semola prove new shape limits in this 2026 math paper. They work on complete Riemannian manifolds, curved spaces with no edge. The key rule is nonnegative Ricci curvature, a mild bound on how the space bends. They also treat RCD spaces, a wider class built for rough settings.

One main result is a rigidity theorem on Betti numbers, counts that track holes in a space. It answers a question open since work by M.-T. Anderson in 1990. A second result is a vanishing theorem for simplicial volume. That result widens a known theorem by another author, whose name is cut off in the abstract.
arxiv-2601-14631:
Jinyang Liao and Ziyang Lyu present a learning framework in this 2026 paper. It is semi-supervised learning for Gaussian mixture modelling under a Missing at Random mechanism. Semi-supervised means some data points carry labels and many do not. Missing at Random describes how the labels come to be missing. Their method explicitly parameterizes the missing-label mechanism.

They model the probability of missingness as a function of classification uncertainty. To quantify that uncertainty, they introduce margin confidence. They also incorporate the Aranda-Ordaz link function, which flexibly captures asymmetric relationships between uncertainty and missing probability. The fix is neat. Doubt is not a flaw in the data here; it is a clue the model can use. Readers get a mixture model that learns from its own doubtful cases instead of ignoring them.
arxiv-2601-14831:
J. McKean, L. Munteanu, and S. Abe benchmark neutrino scattering models in this 2026 paper. They examine three exclusive nuclear ground state shell models implemented in the NEUT neutrino event generator. They benchmark them against the recent JSNS2 measurement of missing energy, made with a monoenergetic neutrino source. A single-energy beam makes the test unusually clean.

The nature of the measurement allows a detailed investigation of nuclear ground-state modeling using a neutrino source. It gives access to a direct measurement of the neutron spectral function in a carbon-12 nucleus. Readers get a rare, sharp check on the nuclear models inside a major neutrino simulation tool.
arxiv-2601-15531:
Felipe Atenas, Minh N. Dao, and Matthew K. Tam build optimization methods in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their topic is structured monotone inclusion problems. These are problems of finding a point where a sum of operators vanishes. Distributed forward-backward splitting is a standard way to attack them. The team's version allows variable stepsizes. Step sizes can change as the method runs.

The framework rests on relocated fixed-point iterations. It extends an approach from a 2025 paper they cite. The extension covers conically averaged operators. That widens the class of methods the theory supports, including graph-based forward-backward schemes. Variable stepsizes can speed convergence in practice. A theory that certifies them helps users trust the faster runs.
arxiv-2601-15631:
Xingzhou Chen and a large team report an optical effect in a layered material in a 2026 arXiv paper. Atomically thin transition-metal dichalcogenides carry a valley degree of freedom. It works like a binary index, fit for storing information. Bare valley excitons live briefly and move poorly, which limits their use. Coupling them with light forms exciton-polaritons. These hybrids offer a route past those limits.

The team reports an anomalous optical valley Hall effect. Their system is a monolayer of WS2 in the polariton regime. A Hall effect here means valley types drift apart under a drive. Anomalous behavior hints at physics beyond the plain version. Valley-based devices remain a research goal. Effects that steer valleys with light are steps toward that goal.
arxiv-2601-15731:
Linyong Zou and a large team improve a brain-imaging method in a 2026 arXiv paper. The method is electrophysiological source imaging, or ESI. It locates brain activity from scalp signals. ESI is an essential technique for diagnosing brain disorders. Model-based and deep learning methods have made promising progress. Precise imaging still hinges on choosing and refining features well. That step remains a central challenge, the authors say.

Their method is FAIR-ESI. The name expands to feature adaptive importance refinement. It adapts which features matter as imaging proceeds. Better feature handling should sharpen the source maps clinicians read. For epilepsy and other disorders, a sharper map can change care. The paper targets that refinement step directly.
arxiv-2601-15831:
Faruk Pasic and five co-authors analyze beamforming with cheap converters in a 2026 arXiv paper. Future wireless systems will use MIMO beamforming at millimeter-wave bands. Those bands deliver high data rates. Fully digital beamforming gives flexible spatial processing. It suits latency-critical applications well. It also depends on accurate channel estimation. Every antenna path needs its own data converters in a digital design.

High-resolution converters are costly and power-hungry at these speeds. The paper studies low-resolution DACs and ADCs instead. Coarser conversion saves power but adds error. The question is how much performance survives the savings. For network gear makers, that trade-off decides real products. The analysis speaks to 6G hardware planning.
arxiv-2601-14931:
Nouhoum Coulibaly, Ousmane Ly, Michael Leventhal, and Ousmane Goro study generative AI in Mali. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks if such tools can help build peace stories. It also asks if they can help revive the country's musical heritage.

The study sits in a hard setting. Tensions between groups and deep social splits shape daily life there. Those splits drive a search for new shared frames that can aid reconciliation. The authors test in depth what AI-made music and story work can add to that search for common ground and trust.
arxiv-2601-15131:
Ayan Maity and Sudeshna Sarkar plan delivery routes against the clock. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the vehicle routing problem under a finite time horizon. The goal is to serve as many customer requests as possible before time runs out.

The authors use deep reinforcement learning for the task. Their key piece is a new routing network embedding module. It builds local vectors for each node in the route graph. It also builds a global view of the graph that knows the context. Those two views guide the agent's choices.
arxiv-2601-15231:
Hanchen Wang, Junfeng Hu, and a large team report the first direct sighting of antimagnons. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with spin waves in magnetic materials. An antimagnon is a spin wave with negative energy, marked by a dispersion curve that runs the wrong way round in momentum space.

The team used Brillouin light scattering spectroscopy to catch that signature. Their sample is an ultrathin BiYIG film. Its perpendicular anisotropy just cancels the demagnetizing field. In that tuned state, the inverted dispersion shows up clearly, giving direct spectroscopic proof of antimagnons.
arxiv-2601-15331:
Rishit Chugh probes language models with hostile prompts, and counts the cost of doing so. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with jailbreaking: prompt tricks that push a model to produce outputs it should refuse. Wide deployment has raised the security stakes.

Models out of the box often lack robust guardrails. Manual exploits take time and effort to craft. Chugh presents RECAP, a resource-efficient method for adversarial prompting. It aims to test a model's defenses at scale without the heavy cost of hand-built attacks crafted fresh by hand on each new system.
arxiv-2601-16031:
Galen Bergsten and seven coauthors ask how hidden partner stars skew counts of small planets. Their 2026 preprint uses data from the Kepler space craft. A close star that is not seen on its own can make a planet look too small. It can also make the planet look more easy to find than it is. Both flaws bend the rate at which small worlds seem to occur.

To size the second flaw, the team picked 198 Kepler stars. Each star could show an Earth like world if it stood alone. The team then took sharp views of those stars with ground optics. The views test how often a hidden mate was in fact there. The work helps clean up planet counts for small worlds.
arxiv-2601-16231:
Aafiya Hussain and four coauthors test sound only attacks on models that join three modes. Their 2026 preprint deals with models that take sound, pics and words. Such models score well on thought and build tasks. Their strength when sound is bent with ill will is less known. The team bends sound in ways a hearer may not note.

Bent sound aims to throw the joint model off its true pick. The attack needs no change to pics or words at all. If sound alone breaks the model, guards must watch sound most. The study maps that risk in a set, step by step way. It warns build teams of a blind spot.
arxiv-2601-16431:
Ruonan Zheng and three coauthors set test plans for Kriging models of costly runs. Their 2026 preprint deals with stand in models for hard lab runs. Comp runs now stand in for real tests in much build work. A Kriging model then stands in for the comp run. Good test points cut the gap of the stand in across the whole space.

Step by step plans add points where the gap is most large. Each new run then trims the worst flaw in the model. Trim plans save runs while they lift trust in the stand in. The work sorts plans by how fast they close the gap. It serves teams with tight run counts.
arxiv-2601-16831:
Shangjie Tian, Qi Wang, and a team of co-authors squeeze a crystal to make it lossless. The crystal Ge2Bi2Te5 blocks current flow in a rare, twist-tied way. Such twist traits make it a topological insulator. Their 2026 preprint tracks the crystal's flow traits under huge force. They also swap in manganese atoms to add magnetism.

Force can flip such crystals into superconductors. The swap of atoms shifts that flip in clear ways. The team maps how the flip point moves with the swap. States that mix pairing and twist could host new quantum bits. High-force maps guide the hunt for those states.
arxiv-2601-16931:
Mauro D'Onofrio, Francesco Brevi, Cesare Chiosi, and Paola Marziani draw a wide view of galaxy scale links. Galaxies of unlike shapes still share tight links. Size, mass, and spin tie in set ways. Their 2026 preprint pulls those links from two big sky surveys. WINGS and MANGA give the base facts for the work.

The team sorts galaxies by shape in the link planes. Each zone of a plane gets a share count. Model data from Illustris joins the view as a check. Shared links test how galaxies grew and aged. Shape-wise gaps can flag where growth tales fall short.
arxiv-2601-17131:
Ondřej Kubíček, Viliam Lisý, and Tuomas Sandholm sharpen game play by use of fine tie rules. Big games are played from a pre-set plan, then tuned live. In hid-fact games, the live tune must weigh unseen states. It must also weigh the foe's past plan. Their 2026 preprint adds equilibrium refinements to that tune step. Such refinements pick the best of tied best replies.

Fine picks can lift the tune past the base plan. They curb plays that a smart foe could exploit. Games here span cards, bids, and guard work. Sharp subgame tools push AI skill in all three.
arxiv-2601-17331:
Fabian Vazquez and seven co-authors work on finding polyps in colonoscopy images. Polyps can grow into colorectal cancer, so early finds save lives. Computer tools help doctors spot them in scans. U-Net style models, in CNN, Transformer, and Mamba forms, already score well. They still miss shape and structure cues. Low contrast and clutter make those cues hard to read.

The team adds geometric priors to guide the models. Priors tell the network what shapes to expect. That help should sharpen borders in messy scenes. Sharper maps mean fewer missed polyps. The work serves computer-aided diagnosis in real clinics. It aims at the cases where current tools are weakest.
arxiv-2601-17431:
H. Kemal İlter audits how AI help can decay the facts in survey papers. Language models make writing faster. They can also add informational entropy, a slow blur of truth. İlter ran a forensic audit of 50 recent AI survey papers. The set held 5,514 citations from late 2024 to early 2026. He tracked how valid citation chains degrade.

The title names a 17 percent gap. That figure sums up the decay he found. Hallucinated papers are a known flaw; broken chains are quieter. They let false claims look sourced and sound. The audit gives editors a scale for the harm. It argues for citation checks as a core step, not an extra.
arxiv-2601-17531:
José Manuel Casas, Emzar Khmaladze, and Manuel Ladra study Leibniz n-algebras. These algebras generalize Leibniz algebras to higher arity. The authors analyze forgetful functors and the Daletskii-Takhtajan functor. They focus on perfect objects and crossed modules in this setting. Functors move results between categories in algebra.

They then apply the work to homology and universal central extensions. Central extensions are a core tool to classify algebras. Homology reads the deep shape of such structures. Clear functor behavior makes those tools safe to move. The paper serves pure algebra. It firms up a young field where base results are still being set. Each firm base saves later work.
arxiv-2601-17831:
Zehao Liu, Xiyan Peng, Zhenghong Tang, Zhaoxiang Qi, Shilong Liao, and Yong Yu rework an old sky survey to find stars it missed. Their 2026 preprint describes a software pipeline for 2MASS, the Two Micron All Sky Survey. The pipeline re-runs detection on the survey's J-band images. It tunes the search settings and adds a screening step that weighs signal strength and image sharpness together.

That joint screen helps pick out faint point sources that the first pass left behind. A first paper in a series, it sets up the method and its gains. Faint objects matter for maps of the Galaxy and for counts of cool, dim stars. Old survey data can still yield new finds when read with fresh tools.
arxiv-2601-18331:
Junmo Jeon and Shiro Sakai extend the idea of hyperuniformity from classical matter into quantum electron systems. Their 2026 preprint builds a framework on that extension. Hyperuniform systems hide their disorder: density fluctuations shrink at large scales. The quantum version adds the intrinsic fluctuations of many-body ground states. The team studies long-wavelength fluctuations through the charge-density structure factor. A quantity called the quantum weight enters, tied to the system's gap structure.

The framework can flag quantum phase transitions. It also reveals gaps that other probes may miss. A new lens on ground states serves the study of quantum materials. The work joins two fields that grew up apart.
arxiv-2601-18931:
Frederick Tsz-Ho Fong and Hung Tran follow a flow that slowly reshapes curved spaces. Ricci flow deforms a shape's metric over time, much as heat evens out warmth. The pair study it on bundles built over products of special curved spaces called Kähler-Einstein manifolds.

Their starting metric comes from a known ansatz, a structured guess used in past work. They prove the flow keeps that structure as it runs, which tames a hard equation into parts that can be tracked. Keeping the ansatz lets them say how the shape evolves and what it may settle toward in the long run.
arxiv-2601-19231:
Yangyang Guo and four co-authors show that safety training in language models can wash out with harmless data. Aligned models refuse unsafe asks, and those refusals tend to start with a fixed few words, like an apology. That sameness, the team finds, is a crack in the armor.

Fine tuning on a small set of purely benign samples can undo the refusal habit. The study is a warning, not a how-to celebration: guards that rest on surface patterns are fragile. Builders who ship fine tuning to users need defenses that survive contact with ordinary data.
arxiv-2601-19331:
Giovanni Valvassori Bolgè characterizes the corner points of a class of monotone functions, then puts them to work on contests. Extreme points are the shapes that cannot be built by blending others, so knowing them maps a whole family. The family here is multi dimensional and monotone, growing in every direction at once.

He applies the result to large contests, where many players vie for prizes under set rules. The corner point view gives a handy form for the best prize allocation rules across a broad range of tastes about risk and fairness. Contest design, from sales races to grants, rests on such rules.
arxiv-2601-19431:
Markus Seidel, for the CMS Collaboration, reviews the building blocks of particle events in the LHC's third run. CMS is one of the two great detectors at the Large Hadron Collider, now colliding at higher energy in Run 3. Its physics objects are the reconstructed leptons, photons, jets, and missing momentum that every analysis starts from.

Their performance and calibration decide the quality of all CMS science. Run 3 piles many collisions into each crossing, so the algorithms must stay sharp in a crowd. Seidel's review tells analysts exactly how these objects behave and where their limits sit.
arxiv-2601-19531:
Alex Mauch-Soriano and nine colleagues ask how many Jupiter-like planets should circle white dwarfs. White dwarfs are the dense embers left when stars like the Sun die. Giant planets are common around living stars, and some are known around evolved stars. Yet only a handful have been found near white dwarfs, despite careful imaging surveys.

The team predicts how often such planets should occur if they survive the star's death. Their forecast can be compared with what surveys actually see. A gap between the two would point to planets being destroyed or thrown out as the star ages. A match would mean the planets mostly endure. Either way, the count tells us how planetary systems end. The work guides future searches around dead stars.
arxiv-2601-19731:
Massimiliano Di Penta and a large group of colleagues write on behalf of SIGSOFT, the software engineering research community's main society. Their subject is the future of the field itself. Conferences keep growing, and with size come rising costs and stale formats. Those barriers shut out many researchers, especially from poorer regions.

That exclusion threatens the inclusivity and global diversity behind the field's success. The authors set out the society's perspective on what must change. The piece is a position statement rather than a research result. It aims to steer community debate about venues, formats, and access. Anyone planning the next decade of software engineering meetings is its intended reader.
arxiv-2601-19831:
Michael Y. Hu, Jane Pan, Ayush Rajesh Jhaveri, Nicholas Lourie, and Kyunghyun Cho study how language models improve with scale. Neural scaling laws predict that overall performance rises smoothly with compute. Validation loss follows tidy power-law curves. But single downstream tasks behave far less tidily: some improve steadily, others plateau, and some get worse with scale.

The authors call their study neural neural scaling laws, a play on modelling the models themselves. Understanding per-task curves matters for anyone deciding how big a model to train. Aggregate laws can hide tasks that matter to real users. Task-level prediction would make compute budgets smarter. The work urges the field to look beneath the smooth averages.
arxiv-2601-19931:
Sebastien Kawada and Dylan Holyoak describe a system entered in a shared task on story similarity. SemEval-2026 Task 4 asks systems to judge how similar two narratives are. Their entry, CascadeMind, mixes neural and symbolic methods in a cascade. The neural part uses a language model that votes many times in parallel, a technique called self-consistency voting.

A supermajority threshold settles confident cases at once. Uncertain cases escalate to more voting rounds. A symbolic ensemble that analyses narrative structure at several scales acts as tiebreaker. Cascades spend heavy computation only where doubt remains. The design reflects a wider pattern in applied AI: fast neural judgement, checked by slower structured analysis.
arxiv-2601-20131:
Deep Shah, Sanket Badhe, and Nehal Kathrotia map out the design choices behind embedding retrieval systems. These tools find matching text or images by meaning. Their paper walks down the full design stack, layer by layer. At the top sits the representation layer, where loss functions and model shapes define what counts as a good match.

The authors contrast bi-encoders, which encode query and item apart, with cross-encoders, which read both together. Each choice trades speed against accuracy in a different way. Their taxonomy names the common pitfalls in these choices, and it gives builders a clear map for weighing cost against quality.
arxiv-2601-20531:
Saurabh Verma and Shivam Dubey prove weaker quantization dimension results for self-similar measures. Quantization asks how well a probability measure can be approximated by finitely many points, and its dimension describes how the error shrinks. The authors study measures whose generating system does not satisfy the usual separation condition.

They use the fact that a subsystem at some level does separate. They also study approximation of the space of Borel probability measures under geometric mean error. Results of this kind extend quantization theory to overlapping fractals, which arise often in practice. These are quiet proofs, but they let the rest of the field build with trust.
arxiv-2601-20631:
Gianluca Allinson and a large team review Rydberg-atom receivers and their potential for space applications. These sensors convert radio, microwave, and terahertz fields into optical signals. They offer calibration traceable to fundamental constants, high sensitivity, and broad tunability.

The review compares five receiver architectures, from Autler-Townes and AC-Stark schemes to superheterodyne and fluorescence designs, against the needs of space missions. Rydberg receivers could give satellites a single sensor for many bands. The assessment helps mission planners judge where the technology is ready and where it is not. One sensor for many bands would cut weight, and weight is cost on any launch to space. The team weighs each design on that scale.
arxiv-2601-18431:
S. Kumano turns to a second spin topic: how the core of an atom shifts the traits of the parts inside it. Work on that shift goes back to a shock find in the early eighties, when tests showed that quarks in a heavy core do not act like quarks in a lone proton. Most past work charted one curve that sums over all spin states.

Kumano looks at a finer split, the gap between two curves tied to how the beam and the target line up. The deuteron, with one proton and one neutron, is the best test bed for that split. Small shifts there can tell us how the strong force bends when parts sit close in a core. The note maps what is known and what new tests could pin down.
arxiv-2601-18631:
Mingyang Song and six colleagues give sight-and-text models a way to call on tools as they think. A person who hits a hard task picks up a tool: a lens, a map, a count aid. A model can do the same if it knows which tool to pick, when to call it, and how to chain calls over steps. That skill is hard when the tool or the task is new.

Their tool, daReasoner, learns to run that chain on the fly. It picks a tool, reads what comes back, and picks the next step from the gain. A good chain could lift scores on tasks that mix sight, facts, and steps. It could also make the model's path clear for staff to check. Tool use of this kind is a key step toward agents that work in the real world.
arxiv-2601-21331:
Filippo Portera proposes a new loss function for support vector machines and neural networks. Loss functions steer training by scoring how wrong a model is. A convex loss is prized because it avoids bad local traps during the search.

The author derives the paired dual problems for both sorting and regression tasks. Tests run on several small datasets, since support vector methods scale poorly to large ones. The new loss aims to keep the good math of classic methods while behaving better in practice. Small, careful tests show where the trade-offs land.
arxiv-2601-21631:
Nicolas Pope and Matti Tedre turn language model training from a black box into a classroom sandbox. Most lessons on generative AI only let students prompt a finished model. The data and mechanics that shape the model stay hidden, which feeds both hype and fear.

The authors built a browser tool where students train a small transformer on their own device. Every step of training is visible and touchable. Students can swap the training text and watch behavior change. Seeing a model learn from data they chose gives a grounded sense of what these systems are and are not.
arxiv-2601-21731:
Kaustubh Sharma, Srijan Tiwari, Ojasva Nema, and Parikshit Pareek extract readable kernels from networks fitted on synthetic data. Such prior-data fitted networks do fast, learned inference, but their priors and kernels stay hidden inside. That opacity blocks uses like surrogate optimization, which need an explicit covariance model.

The authors build a framework that recovers the spectral story of the learned kernel. A decoupled attention design helps separate the pieces. Making the kernel visible turns a black-box predictor into a tool other methods can build on. It also lets users check whether the learned prior matches the problem at hand.
arxiv-2601-22331:
Aditya Narayan Ravi, Snehal Vadvalkar, Abhishek Pandey, and Ilan Shomorony fix a flaw in cell imaging that can hide real drug effects. Cell Painting stains cells so a microscope can read their shape and state in fine detail. Their 2026 preprint notes that lab, tool, and protocol shifts add batch effects that swamp the true signal.

Their fix uses kernels that shift with each batch, plus smart sampling to keep the cost low. Clean data let teams spot how a drug changes cells. The method aims to scale to huge screens. It serves the hunt for new medicines.
arxiv-2601-22531:
Jiayi Dai and Randy Goebel train networks that show their reasons as they decide. Their 2026 preprint works on rationale extraction: one network picks the key input parts, a second decides from those parts alone. The design makes the logic open to view by construction.

A teacher model, the rationalist of the title, guides the learner with step-wise, readable reasons. Such guidance aims for reasons that are both true to the model and clear to people. The need is sharpest in high-stakes fields like health and law. The work seeks trust through shown work.
arxiv-2601-22631:
En Fu, Yanyan Hu, Changhua Hu, Zengwang Jin, and Kaixiang Peng predict how much useful life a machine has left, from little data. Such forecasts guide repairs, yet they have long needed heaps of past wear data from twin machines. Their 2026 preprint, PEFT-MuTS, takes a leaner path.

Their frame fine-tunes only a small part of a model, across many signals at once. Small-data forecasts could serve rare or new gear, where twins do not exist. The work cuts the data bill for a key factory task. It also aims to keep accuracy high. Less data, same warning time, is the goal.
arxiv-2601-21831:
Daniel Gonzalez-Alvarado, Jonas Cassel, Stefania Petra, and Christoph Schnörr work on generating discrete data, such as categories and counts. Generative models usually learn in smooth spaces, which fits awkwardly with data that come in separate bins. Their 2026 preprint builds the learning space from the geometry of categorical distributions themselves.

The authors place a low-dimensional latent space inside the parameter space of product manifolds of categorical distributions. That latent space captures how the variables depend on each other while dropping redundant degrees of freedom. A well-shaped latent space lets a model generate new discrete samples that respect the patterns in the real data. Which matters for survey data, genetics, and other fields built on categories.
arxiv-2601-21931:
Karel Devriendt, Ignacio Echave-Sustaeta Rodríguez, and Frank Röttger work on the statistics of extremes. Hüsler-Reiss distributions are a parametric family used to model multivariate Pareto data, the joint behavior of several variables when all are large at once. A key question is when extremes in some variables tell nothing about extremes in others.

That property is extremal conditional independence. The authors introduce two set functions, which assign values to a distribution and to each of its marginals. They show that independence statements of this kind can be characterized through those functions, using modular structure. Their 2026 preprint gives risk modelers a cleaner test for dependence among rare events, such as joint floods or simultaneous market crashes.
arxiv-2601-22031:
Junhao Ruan and co-authors merge two rival ways of generating text. Autoregressive models write one token at a time, which trains efficiently but decodes slowly. Diffusion language models generate in parallel and run fast, but their training is less direct.

Their 2026 preprint proposes Causal Autoregressive Diffusion, or CARD. It reshapes the diffusion process inside a strictly causal attention mask, so every token still only sees what came before. That design enables dense, per-token supervision in a single forward pass, combining autoregressive training efficiency with diffusion-style throughput at inference. Faster text generation at the same quality would cut serving costs across every product built on language models.
arxiv-2601-22131:
Leonard Papenmeier and Petru Tighineanu speed up optimization problems that pull in opposite directions. Multi-objective optimization balances competing goals with only black-box access to the system and a limited budget of measurements. Many teams hold historical data from related past tasks, which meta-learning could exploit.

Their 2026 preprint presents SMOG, a scalable meta-learning method for multi-objective Bayesian optimization. By learning from earlier tasks, the optimizer starts new problems already knowing where good trade-offs tend to live. That head start matters in drug design, engineering, and materials work. Where each measurement can cost days or thousands of dollars and budgets never stretch as far as the questions do.
arxiv-2601-20831:
Vishnu Sashank Dorbala and Dinesh Manocha give embodied agents a memory that a model actively runs. Their 2026 paper presents MemCtrl. Foundation models personalize their choices through in-context learning. But the context window is small, so memory must be compressed and fetched. Systems like RAG treat memory as a large offline store. That view fits embodied agents poorly.

An embodied agent, such as a robot, works online under tight limits. It has strict memory and compute budgets. MemCtrl uses a multimodal model as an active memory controller instead. The model decides what to keep, drop, and fetch as events unfold. The paper argues this active style suits agents that act in the world. It points toward robots that remember what matters and forget the rest.
arxiv-2512-01531:
Cibran Lopez and co-authors ask why a new class of solar cells lags its promise. Pnictogen chalcohalides soak up light well. They are non-toxic and can be made at low heat. Yet top cells stay well below ten percent efficiency. Their ideal cap is far higher.

The team blames defects in the material. Defects trap charge and waste light energy as heat. They map which defects hurt most. That map tells makers what to fix first in growth. Fixing the worst defects could lift these green cells toward real use in roofs and farms.
arxiv-2512-00931:
Imane Jaaouine and Ross King run a pilot study on a failure mode of AI summaries in a 2025 paper. Large language models sometimes hallucinate, writing output that clashes with the user's prompt or source. In science writing, such context inconsistency can quietly distort findings.

Their project asks whether prompt engineering can cut these errors in zero-shot summarisation of scientific texts. Zero-shot means the model gets no examples and works from pretraining alone. If careful prompting helps, it would be a cheap defense for students and researchers who use AI to digest papers. The pilot design shows how such claims should be tested.
arxiv-2512-01131:
M Martí Massó Moreno, C Pérez-Alanis, and P Manoharan generalize a model for solar eruptions in a 2025 paper. Interplanetary coronal mass ejections are huge clouds of solar material that travel through space. Scientists model them as flux ropes, twisted bundles of magnetic field, to rebuild their shape and field from spacecraft data.

Their generalized elliptical-cylindrical flux rope model allows a nonzero poloidal component in the internal magnetic field, a part older models set aside. A two-step method separates the geometric fit from the magnetic field fit. That split should improve stability and consistency when fitting real events.
arxiv-2601-23131:
Christiaan P. Opperman, Anna S. Bosman, and Katherine M. Malan survey methods that help neural networks generalize. Networks ace many tasks, yet they can stumble on data they have not seen. A large family of tricks, called regularisation, has grown up over the years to fight that weakness.

The authors review those approaches and test them empirically side by side. A clear map of what works, and at what cost, saves practitioners from folklore. Generalization is the difference between a demo and a tool people can rely on. The empirical analysis keeps the survey honest, testing whether celebrated techniques still earn their place in current practice.
arxiv-2601-23231:
George Webber, Alexander Denker, Riccardo Barbano, and Andrew J Reader solve inverse problems with flow-based models under model predictive control. Flow models provide strong priors for rebuilding hidden images from measurements. Guiding them toward a specific measurement, though, is computationally heavy.

Casting guidance as optimal control is elegant but demands costly differentiation through the flow. Their predictive control scheme seeks the same guidance at lower memory and compute cost. Cheaper conditional generation helps medical imaging and other reconstruction tasks. Model predictive control sidesteps repeated differentiation through the flow dynamics, the cost that made control-based guidance heavy.
arxiv-2512-00631:
Multivariate time series modeling is stuck between Gaussian models and one-off models built for single applications. Jonas Andersson and Dimitris Karlis develop maximum likelihood estimation for the VARTA model in 2025. The name promises a vector autoregressive model that can be transformed to anything.

VARTA rests on an underlying, unobserved Gaussian vector autoregression, transformed to match the data's actual distributions. One general approach could serve finance, environment, and industry data alike. Careful likelihood estimation is what turns that elegant construction into a tool practitioners can fit and trust. Transforming to anything means the margins can be counts, positives, or bounded scores. Maximum likelihood gives the estimates a standard theory of uncertainty. For folks who fit such data, the gain is one frame for many kinds of counts. It can bend to fit the shape at hand, yet stay a single tool.
arxiv-2512-03231:
Power spectra of galaxies encode the universe's history. F. Qin and a large team use them to measure cosmic growth in this 2025 work. The work is part of the DESI first data release peculiar velocity survey.

The team measures the auto and cross power spectra of galaxy density and momentum fields. From those spectra they estimate cosmological parameters. This route uses the full pattern of clustering, not just average motions. It offers an independent check on growth rates found by other DESI methods. Spectrum methods capture clustering shape, adding detail beyond average growth numbers.
arxiv-2512-03331:
A nearby red galaxy offers a rare radio detection. L. F. Rodriguez and I. F. Mirabel report it in this 2025 work. The Webb telescope found huge numbers of Little Red Dots in the early universe, compact red galaxies with odd traits.

One odd trait is that no radio signals had been seen from distant Little Red Dots. A local example that does emit radio waves gives a closer test case. Studying it may reveal what powers these objects. That could clarify whether they hide black holes or intense star birth. A local case can be studied in depth that distant, faint dots do not yet allow.
arxiv-2512-03431:
A rare decay of the neutral pion gets its best measure yet. S. Prakhov and a large team report the measurement in this 2025 work. The Dalitz decay turns a pion into an electron, a positron, and a gamma ray.

The team used the A2 tagged-photon facility at the Mainz Microtron. They measured the decay in a photon-proton reaction with the highest statistical accuracy so far. Precise Dalitz data test theory of how pions are built. They also help calibrate detectors used in other particle studies. Tagged photons give clean initial states, which is why the Mainz setup suits rare decays.
arxiv-2512-03531:
A supernova showed helium-rich material around it, a first of its kind. Xiang-Cun Meng and Philipp Podsiadlowski explain that case in this 2025 work. SN 2020eyj is the first type Ia supernova with a signature of compact helium-rich circumstellar material.

Such a large amount of material is hard to explain if the donor star was a helium star. The authors propose a helium common-envelope wind scenario. Their account reshapes how some type Ia explosions are understood. Those explosions are key distance markers for the universe. Helium-rich shells are rare, so each well-modeled case tests donor star theories hard.
arxiv-2512-02031:
Drug hunters often start from a molecule known to bind a target and search libraries for new ones with a similar binding pattern. Omar Mahmood and four co-authors present a 2025 method that learns these patterns, called pharmacophores, directly on three-dimensional voxel grids.

The classic search is brute force: compare the known binder against a huge library with some similarity metric, one candidate at a time. Learning on voxel grids lets a model absorb the spatial arrangement of chemical features that makes binding work. Better search tools mean promising, structurally fresh drug candidates can surface earlier in discovery.
arxiv-2512-02531:
Ming Li and three co-authors study how quantum devices are read out through a faint reflected signal. Dispersive readout is a workhorse of quantum technology, used to learn a qubit state without touching it directly. Here the probe field is a squeezed vacuum, sent in a time symmetric way.

The team builds a full counting statistics framework, which tracks the whole spread of outcomes, not just averages. They pair it with a generalized mean field method suited to open, lossy dynamics. The analysis shows how much measurement information such a readout can deliver, guiding future quantum hardware design. The full spread of counts tells more than a lone mean could ever say on its own.
arxiv-2512-02831:
Ali Alvandi and Mina Rezaei revisit the theory of contrastive learning when test classes differ from training ones. Contrastive methods pull similar samples together and push unlike ones apart in a learned space. That recipe powers much of modern self supervised representation learning.

Standard theory assumes downstream classes come from the same latent distribution as pretraining. Domain generalization breaks that assumption, since the target world shifts. The authors rebuild the analysis for shifted settings. Sounder theory tells practitioners when contrastive pretraining should transfer, and when it may quietly fail. A shift in the world is the rule in real use, so tests that own shift tell us far more than clean room scores.
plos-pone-0010031:
The authors were Ertugrul Dalkic, Xuewei Wang, Neil Wright, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study treated cancer drugs as a network. Earlier network work mapped drugs, targets, and diseases on a huge scale. A smaller network lets analysts look closely at each link and member.

The team built that focused view of links between cancer drugs and their targets. Patterns in the map can hint at new uses for known drugs or risky drug pairings. The approach shows how math from network science can guide cancer research choices. Readers get both the map and the reasoning behind it.
plos-pone-0010231:
The authors were Gabriela Gutierrez-Reyes, Maria Garcia de Leon, Gustavo Varela-Fascinetto, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined livers from very sick children. In adults with cirrhosis, worn-out liver cells that have stopped dividing, called senescent cells, are common. The team asked whether the same is true in children with end stage liver disease.

They studied livers from five children aged three years or less. They measured how often senescent cells appeared and checked cell cycle control points. Finding early cell aging in young livers could change how doctors read the course of childhood liver disease.
plos-pone-0010331:
Kelvin Wong offered a fresh look at bargaining in a 2010 PLOS ONE article on game theory. Bargaining problems ask how two sides can split gains fairly. Wong used geometry, the math of shapes and positions, to frame the question. He sought the outcome where no other deal makes everyone better off at once. In his setup, a balance point is a set of choices with a special property.

At that point, no single player can switch choices and raise the total payoff for the group. The approach gives negotiators a clean way to judge proposed deals. It also links a social problem, dividing gains, to a visual method. Readers get a new lens on an old puzzle in economics and strategy.
plos-pone-0009831:
DNMT1 is an enzyme that copies DNA methylation marks when cells divide. Leonardo D'Aiuto and colleagues took apart one end of the mouse version to see what it does. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The part under study is the N-terminal domain, the front section of the protein. The team used regional frame-shift mutagenesis, small targeted changes that shift how the code is read. Changing pieces one region at a time maps structure to function. The map clarifies how the enzyme keeps methylation patterns stable. Methylation marks help decide which genes stay silent.
plos-pone-0009931:
A protein's address inside the cell decides what jobs it can do. Kuo-Chen Chou and Hong-Bin Shen updated a predictor that guesses those addresses for eukaryotic proteins. The method, Euk-mPLoc 2.0, appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Eukaryotic cells are the complex cells of animals, plants, and fungi.

Subcellular localization means which compartment of the cell a protein lives in. Some proteins sit at a single site, others at multiple sites at once. The new method predicts both cases. Reliable address guesses help biologists interpret the flood of new protein sequences.
